choices: 200 OK — the request succeeded
201 Created — a new resource was created; pair it with a Location header
204 No Content — creation succeeded but there's nothing to return
200 is fine for creation; status codes don't matter to clients
scenarios.hint: Which status code's definition is literally 'a new resource was created as a result of the request'?
scenarios.prompt: What status should the endpoint return?
scenarios.situation: A POST that creates an order returns 200 OK; the API style guide requires the correct creation semantics.
scenarios.title: The created order that says OK
scenarios.why: 201 Created is the semantic status for successful resource creation, conventionally paired with a Location header pointing at the new resource. 200 means 'here's the result of your request' with no creation implied; 204 means success with intentionally empty body. Status codes are machine-readable contracts — clients, caches, and monitoring all branch on them.

choices: The browser blocks all cross-origin requests — the API must be same-origin
The API's response lacks Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and the preflight needs the right Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers) — CORS is enforced by the browser, configured on the server
fetch can't do cross-origin POSTs — use XMLHttpRequest instead
CORS is fixed by adding mode: 'no-cors' — then the response is readable
evidence:
Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/orders' from origin 'https://shop.example.com'
has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header
scenarios.hint: Who enforces CORS — the server or the browser? And where must the permission be granted?
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and where is it fixed?
scenarios.situation: A frontend on shop.example.com can't POST to api.example.com; the console shows a CORS error.
scenarios.title: Blocked by CORS policy
scenarios.why: CORS is a browser-enforced policy: the browser blocks the frontend from reading a cross-origin response unless the server opts in via Access-Control-Allow-Origin (plus Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers on the OPTIONS preflight for non-simple requests). The fix is server-side headers, not client workarounds — mode: 'no-cors' makes the response opaque (unreadable). Also: with credentials: 'include', the origin can't be the wildcard *.

choices: GET /getOrders?userId=7 — action verbs in the path are the REST convention
GET /users/7/orders — nested resources express the relationship; filter/sort/paginate via query params
POST /orders/search with the user id in the body — searches should be POSTs
GET /orders with no params — the client filters the full list
evidence: # TODO: endpoint for a user's orders, newest first, 20 per page
scenarios.hint: Resources are nouns, relationships nest, and non-identifying modifiers ride the query string. What identifies the collection here?
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic endpoint?
scenarios.situation: An API needs a user's orders, newest first, paginated.
scenarios.title: Designing the orders endpoint
scenarios.why: GET /users/7/orders with ?sort=-created_at&page=2&per_page=20 follows REST conventions: plural nouns, nesting for ownership, query params for filtering/sorting/pagination. Action verbs in paths (getOrders) are RPC style; POST-for-search is for complex bodies; returning everything for client-side filtering doesn't scale. Consistent URL design is a usability feature of the API.

choices: Check response.ok and throw/handle on !ok — fetch only rejects on network failures, not HTTP error statuses
Wrap in try/catch — that catches 404s and 500s automatically
Check response.status === 200 exactly — any other status is an error
fetch rejects on 4xx/5xx — no status handling needed
evidence:
const res = await fetch('/api/orders/9999');
const order = await res.json();  // 404 HTML page -> JSON parse error
scenarios.hint: What does the fetch promise do on a 404 — reject, or resolve with a response whose ok is false?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the 404 become a JSON parse error?
scenarios.situation: Fetching a missing order throws a JSON parse error instead of a clean 'not found'.
scenarios.title: The fetch that doesn't throw
scenarios.why: fetch resolves for any HTTP status — including 404 and 500 — and only rejects on network-level failures (DNS, refused connection). The code must inspect response.ok (or status) before parsing; otherwise a 404 HTML error page goes into .json() and explodes. The pattern: if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...) with the status, then parse.

choices: Send the retry immediately — the server will deduplicate automatically
Send an Idempotency-Key header with a client-generated unique key; the server stores the first result per key and replays it for duplicates
Retries are unsafe and must be disabled for POSTs
Use PUT instead of POST — PUT is idempotent so the problem disappears
evidence:
POST /api/payments -> timeout (unknown: did it charge?)
# client must retry, but a double charge is unacceptable
scenarios.hint: The server can't tell 'retry of the same intent' from 'a second charge'. What client-supplied token lets it distinguish them?
scenarios.prompt: How should the client retry safely?
scenarios.situation: A payment POST times out; the client doesn't know if the charge happened.
scenarios.title: The payment that might have happened
scenarios.why: The Idempotency-Key pattern: the client generates a unique key per intent and sends it on the POST; the server persists the key with the first result and replays that result for subsequent requests with the same key. Retrying blindly risks double-charging; PUT's idempotency only helps if the API is designed around it. For money-moving endpoints, idempotency keys are the industry standard.

choices: Poll the endpoint every second — simple and reliable
Use a webhook: the server POSTs to a client-registered URL when the job completes; verify the signature (HMAC) on receipt
Keep the HTTP connection open for the full 10 minutes — long requests are fine
WebSockets are required — webhooks can't deliver results
scenarios.hint: 202 Accepted means 'received, working on it'. How does the client learn when it's done — without asking forever?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right completion-notification design?
scenarios.situation: An export endpoint returns 202; the client needs the result when the 10-minute job finishes.
scenarios.title: The job that takes ten minutes
scenarios.why: 202 Accepted is the correct immediate response for async work; completion notification belongs to a webhook (server calls the client's registered URL) rather than polling (wasteful) or holding connections open (fragile). The critical companion: verify the webhook signature (HMAC of the payload with a shared secret) so attackers can't forge completion events.

choices: Store the token in a global variable — globals persist across renders
Keep the token in component state (or context) and attach it via an API client wrapper/interceptor that sets the Authorization header on every request
Put the token in the URL query string — headers are unreliable
localStorage is only for strings — tokens must be objects, so it can't be used
evidence: // TODO: attach the JWT to every API call after login
scenarios.hint: Every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. What pattern applies that header in one place instead of at every call site?
scenarios.prompt: How should the token be attached to requests?
scenarios.situation: After login, every API call must carry the JWT.
scenarios.title: The token on every request
scenarios.why: Centralize it: an API client module (or fetch/axios interceptor) reads the stored token and sets Authorization: Bearer on each request. Scattering header logic across call sites guarantees one forgotten call. (Storage choice — memory vs localStorage vs HttpOnly cookie — is a separate XSS-vs-CSRF tradeoff; the attachment pattern is the same.)

choices: Call .json() on the response in the component and pass the parsed object down
Define the expected shape (TypeScript interface or Zod schema) and validate/narrow at the API boundary — fail fast on contract drift
Trust the backend — frontend validation of API shapes is redundant
Use `any` for all API responses — flexibility beats rigidity
evidence:
interface Order { id: number; total: number; }
// API actually returns { id, total, currency } and sometimes total as a string
scenarios.hint: The backend changed its shape and the UI broke silently. Where's the cheapest place to catch 'the shape changed' — at the boundary, or deep in a component?
scenarios.prompt: How should the frontend guard against shape drift?
scenarios.situation: A backend change to the order payload breaks the UI at runtime with no compile-time signal.
scenarios.title: The shape that drifted
scenarios.why: Validate at the boundary: a Zod schema (or careful TypeScript narrowing) on API responses turns silent drift into a loud, early failure at the one place data enters. `any` and blind trust push the breakage deep into components where it's mysterious. Types document the contract; runtime validation enforces it — use both at the seam.

choices: Show a generic 'loading' spinner forever — the request might still succeed
Model the request state explicitly (idle/loading/success/error) and render each state — including the error with a retry action
Errors are rare — render nothing on failure
Reload the whole page on any API error — simplest recovery
evidence:
const [orders, setOrders] = useState(null);
// TODO: loading and error states
scenarios.hint: The UI has three possible realities: waiting, data, failure. How many does it currently render?
scenarios.prompt: What states must the UI handle?
scenarios.situation: An orders page shows a blank screen during load and on failure.
scenarios.title: The blank page
scenarios.why: Every remote-data UI has at least three states — loading, success, error — and users need to see each: skeletons/spinners for loading, data for success, and for errors a message plus a retry action (not a blank page or a forced reload). Explicit state machines (or a data-fetching library's status flags) make the missing states impossible to forget.

choices: Debounce the input at 300ms — fewer requests, problem solved
Cancel the previous request (AbortController) or ignore stale responses — only the latest query's results may render
Cache every response forever — stale data is better than wrong data
Disable the search box while a request is in flight — users must wait
scenarios.hint: Responses arrive out of order. What distinguishes the response you want from the ones you don't — its request?
scenarios.prompt: How do you ensure only the latest results render?
scenarios.situation: Fast typing in a search box shows results for an older query.
scenarios.title: The search that answers late
scenarios.why: Without cancellation, a slow response for 'reac' can land after 'react' and overwrite state — the classic async race. AbortController in the effect cleanup cancels the in-flight request on each keystroke; alternatively, tag responses with the query and ignore mismatches. Debouncing reduces frequency but doesn't fix ordering.

choices: Store the draft in component state and lift it via callbacks (or a tiny store) so navigation preserves it — component state dies with the component
Keep it in the step component's useState — React preserves state across route changes
Store it in the URL hash — hashes survive navigation automatically
Drafts can't survive navigation — warn the user instead
evidence: // 3-step checkout wizard; going Back loses the entered data
scenarios.hint: Route changes unmount the step component. Where does its useState go — and what survives unmounting?
scenarios.prompt: How should the wizard preserve entered data?
scenarios.situation: Going back a step in a checkout wizard wipes the entered data.
scenarios.title: The wizard that forgets
scenarios.why: Component state lives and dies with the component — navigating away unmounts the step and destroys its useState. Lift the draft to a parent that persists across steps (wizard shell state, context, or a small store), or persist to the URL/sessionStorage for refresh-survival. The rule: state must live at least as long as the UI that needs it.

choices: Refetch the list after every mutation — simplest and always correct
Update the local list optimistically (or invalidate the query cache) so the UI reflects the mutation without a full refetch round-trip
Mutations don't affect queries — leave the list stale until the user refreshes
Store the list in a global variable and mutate it directly
scenarios.hint: The mutation succeeded but the query cache doesn't know. What tells the cached list that its data changed?
scenarios.prompt: How should the UI reflect the new todo?
scenarios.situation: After adding a todo, the list doesn't update until a manual refresh.
scenarios.title: The todo that didn't appear
scenarios.why: Mutations and queries are separate cache entries: creating a todo doesn't invalidate the ['todos'] query. The fix is invalidation (queryClient.invalidateQueries(['todos'])) or an optimistic update that inserts the item immediately and rolls back on error. Blind refetching works but wastes a round-trip; optimistic updates make the UI feel instant.

choices: Increase the server timeout to 10 minutes — long requests are fine
Return 202 Accepted immediately with a job id; process in a background worker/queue; let the client poll or receive a webhook on completion
Run the export synchronously but stream the response — streaming fixes timeouts
Tell users to export smaller date ranges — the API is fine
evidence:
POST /api/exports ->504 Gateway Timeout after 60s
# report generation takes ~8 minutes
scenarios.hint: HTTP is a bad home for 8-minute computations. What response says 'accepted, working on it' — and where does the work go?
scenarios.prompt: How should the endpoint be redesigned?
scenarios.situation: A report export takes 8 minutes; the request times out at the gateway.
scenarios.title: The eight-minute request
scenarios.why: Long work doesn't belong in the request lifecycle: gateways, load balancers, and clients all time out. The pattern is 202 Accepted with a job id, a background worker (queue + consumer) doing the work, and completion via polling or webhook. Streaming helps for large-but-fast responses, not for compute-bound minutes.

choices: Validate at the API boundary and reject with 400/422 — never let invalid data reach the domain
Validate in the database with CHECK constraints only — the API should accept anything
Validation is the frontend's job — the API trusts its callers
Catch the database error and return 500 — the client learns from the error
evidence:
// POST /api/bookings accepts { seats: -3, date: "yesterday" }
// -> 500 from a deep service-layer crash
scenarios.hint: The 500 came from deep inside. Where's the earliest point that knows what 'valid' means — and what status tells the client it's their fault?
scenarios.prompt: Where should validation live, and what should the client get?
scenarios.situation: Invalid booking input (negative seats, past date) causes a 500 deep in the service.
scenarios.title: Validation at the wrong layer
scenarios.why: Validate at the API boundary: malformed input is a client error (400/422 with field-level messages), not a server crash. Letting it through to deep layers produces 500s that mislead monitoring and leak internals. Defense in depth adds DB constraints too — but the API contract is enforced at the edge, where the client can act on the feedback.

choices: Log the full card number for debugging — logs are internal
Never handle raw card numbers — use a PCI-compliant processor (Stripe/etc.) with tokenization; card data must never touch your servers/logs
Encrypt the card number in the database — encryption equals compliance
Card data is fine in logs if the log server has a firewall
scenarios.hint: What's the cheapest way to achieve PCI compliance for card data — handle it perfectly, or never touch it at all?
scenarios.prompt: How should card payments be architected?
scenarios.situation: A new checkout needs to process credit cards.
scenarios.title: The card number problem
scenarios.why: The winning move is not to play: tokenization via a compliant processor (Stripe Elements, etc.) means raw PANs never touch your servers, logs, or database — collapsing PCI scope from 'prove everything is secure' to a short SAQ. Encrypting-and-storing keeps the full compliance burden; logging PANs is a breach waiting for an audit.

choices: Log at debug level with full request bodies — more data is better
Log structured events with correlation/request ids, appropriate levels, and no secrets — logs must be searchable and safe
console.log everywhere — structured logging is overkill
Logs are only for errors — successful requests need no logging
evidence:
console.log("user " + userId + " did a thing");
// production incident: can't trace a request across services
scenarios.hint: During an incident you need every log line for one request across three services. What ties them together?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the logging, and what replaces it?
scenarios.situation: An incident can't be traced across services; logs are unstructured strings.
scenarios.title: Logs you can't search
scenarios.why: Structured logging (JSON lines with timestamp, level, service, correlation/request id) makes logs queryable: filter by request id and the whole cross-service trail appears. Unstructured string concatenation can't be filtered or aggregated. Rules: propagate a correlation id through the call chain, pick levels deliberately (debug/info/warn/error), and never log secrets, tokens, or PII.

choices: Deploy the new version to all servers at once — fastest feedback
Roll out gradually (canary a slice of traffic, watch metrics, then proceed) with instant rollback — limit the blast radius of a bad deploy
Deploy on Friday evening — the weekend is quiet for monitoring
Skip staging — production is the real test
evidence: # TODO: release v2.4 of the checkout service
scenarios.hint: If v2.4 has a critical bug, how many users should meet it before you notice — all of them, or a canary slice?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe rollout strategy?
scenarios.situation: A checkout service release needs to go out with minimal risk.
scenarios.title: Releasing the checkout
scenarios.why: Canary/blue-green deploys bound the blast radius: route a small percentage to the new version, watch error rates and business metrics, promote or roll back automatically. Big-bang deploys turn every release into an all-or-nothing bet on the busiest service. The rollback path must be as tested as the rollout — 'deploy fast' means 'revert fast'.

choices: Return 500 for every downstream failure — the client's problem
Implement timeouts, retries with backoff (on idempotent calls), and a circuit breaker — fail fast and degrade gracefully instead of cascading
Retry forever until the downstream recovers — persistence pays off
Remove the timeout — waiting longer always resolves it
evidence:
// checkout calls inventory, pricing, and fraud services
// one slow downstream -> all checkout threads pile up -> outage
scenarios.hint: Threads waiting on a hung downstream are threads not serving anyone. What pattern stops calling a service that's clearly down?
scenarios.prompt: How should the service handle downstream failures?
scenarios.situation: A slow inventory service cascades into a full checkout outage.
scenarios.title: The cascade
scenarios.why: Resilience is layered: timeouts bound the wait, retries with exponential backoff + jitter handle transient blips (only on idempotent operations), and the circuit breaker trips after repeated failures — failing fast with a degraded response instead of piling up threads. Without the breaker, one sick dependency takes down every caller: the definition of a cascading failure.

choices: Add an index on every column — indexes are always beneficial
Add an index on (status, created_at) matching the query's filter and sort — then verify with EXPLAIN that it's used
Indexes don't help WHERE clauses — only ORDER BY
Partition the table — indexes can't fix 10M rows
evidence:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 50;
-- 8.2s on 10M rows; EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan
scenarios.hint: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. What data structure lets the database jump to 'pending' rows in created_at order without reading all 10M?
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and how do you confirm it?
scenarios.situation: An orders query takes 8 seconds; EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan.
scenarios.title: The eight-second query
scenarios.why: A composite index on (status, created_at) serves both the equality filter and the ordering from the index, turning 10M-row scans into a targeted range read. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) before and after proves the plan changed. Index-everything is wrong — indexes cost write performance and storage; the right index matches the query's access pattern.

choices: Use SELECT * with a JOIN and deduplicate in code — simplest
JOIN orders to customers and aggregate in SQL (GROUP BY customer) — the database is built for exactly this
Two separate queries and a nested loop in code — avoid JOINs, they're slow
Denormalize everything into one table — joins are a design smell
evidence: -- TODO: revenue per customer for Q3
scenarios.hint: You need one row per customer with a sum. Is that a job for the database's aggregation engine or for application loops?
scenarios.prompt: How should the query be written?
scenarios.situation: Revenue per customer for a quarter is needed from orders and customers tables.
scenarios.title: Revenue per customer
scenarios.why: JOIN + GROUP BY with SUM is the database's home turf: one round-trip, set-based aggregation, the optimizer's choice of hash/sort strategies. Pulling both tables into code for a nested loop ships megabytes to do what the engine does in milliseconds. ('JOINs are slow' is a myth — missing indexes are slow; the join itself is the relational model's core operation.)

choices: Wrap each statement in its own transaction — more transactions equal more safety
Wrap the transfer in a single transaction (BEGIN; debit; credit; COMMIT;) — ACID guarantees both-or-neither
Transactions are automatic — no explicit boundaries needed
Use two connections, one per statement — parallelism is faster
scenarios.hint: A crash between the two UPDATEs destroys money. What boundary makes them atomic?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the transfer atomic?
scenarios.situation: A funds transfer does two UPDATEs; a crash between them loses money.
scenarios.title: The half transfer
scenarios.why: A single transaction makes the debit+credit atomic: either both commit or neither does (with rollback on failure) — the A in ACID. Autocommit mode commits each statement separately, which is exactly the money-destroying behavior. Explicit BEGIN/COMMIT (or the driver's transaction block) is the unit of consistency for multi-statement operations.

choices: Store the tags as a comma-separated string in the product row — one table, simple
A junction table product_tags(product_id, tag_id) with foreign keys — the normalized many-to-many
A JSON array column of tag names — flexible and queryable
One boolean column per tag — explicit and fast
evidence: -- products can have many tags; tags apply to many products
scenarios.hint: Many-to-many with attributes on neither side alone. Which relational structure represents 'pairs' without duplication?
scenarios.prompt: How should the schema model it?
scenarios.situation: Products and tags are many-to-many; the schema is undecided.
scenarios.title: Products, tags, and pairs
scenarios.why: A junction table with two foreign keys (composite primary key) is the normalized many-to-many: no duplication, referential integrity both ways, and room for relationship attributes (tagged_at). Comma-separated strings break querying and integrity; JSON columns are fine for schemaless payloads but lose FK guarantees; boolean-per-tag doesn't scale. Normalization isn't dogma — it's the structure that prevents update anomalies.

choices: Run migrations explicitly as a deploy step (migrate before the new code serves) — schema and code stay in lockstep
Edit the production schema by hand when needed — fastest
Let the ORM auto-migrate on startup (sync) — automation handles it
Migrations are only for development — production schemas are managed separately
scenarios.hint: The new code expects the new column. If the code deploys before the column exists, what happens on the first request?
scenarios.prompt: How should schema changes ship?
scenarios.situation: A deploy needs a new column; the pipeline has no migration step.
scenarios.title: Code without its column
scenarios.why: Migrations run as an explicit deploy step before the new code takes traffic — the schema the code was written against must exist when it runs. Hand-editing production drifts untracked; ORM auto-sync on startup races across instances and can destroy data. For zero-downtime, expand-then-contract (add column, deploy, backfill, then remove) — but the baseline is: migrate, then serve.

choices: Relational for everything — NoSQL is a fad
A document store for the catalog (flexible, read-heavy product data) and relational for orders/inventory (transactions, integrity) — match the store to the access pattern
Key-value for everything — simplest model
The team should only ever use one database — polyglot persistence is unmaintainable
evidence:
# catalog: 2M products, flexible attributes, read-heavy
# orders: money movement, strict integrity
scenarios.hint: One workload needs flexible schemas and fast reads; the other needs ACID and joins. Must one database serve both?
scenarios.prompt: How should the data be split?
scenarios.situation: A platform has a read-heavy flexible catalog and transactional order data.
scenarios.title: One database or two?
scenarios.why: Polyglot persistence matches stores to workloads: a document store fits the catalog's flexible, read-heavy shape; the relational database fits orders' transactional integrity (ACID, joins, constraints). One-database dogma forces one workload into the wrong model. The cost — two systems to operate — is real, so the split must earn it: here the access patterns genuinely differ.

choices: MD5(password) — fast and simple
bcrypt/argon2 with per-password salts — adaptive, slow hashes that resist brute force
SHA-256 with a site-wide salt — one salt is enough
Base64-encode the password — encoding obscures it
scenarios.hint: GPUs try billions of hashes per second. What property must the hash function have to make each guess expensive?
scenarios.prompt: How should passwords be stored?
scenarios.situation: A new auth system needs password storage.
scenarios.title: Storing passwords, again
scenarios.why: Adaptive hashes (bcrypt, argon2, scrypt) are deliberately slow and salted per password — each guess costs real time, defeating GPU brute force, and salts defeat rainbow tables. Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256) fall in hours; a site-wide salt still allows parallel attacks; encoding is not hashing. The work factor should rise as hardware improves.

choices: Decode the JWT payload and trust the role claim — the signature is optional
Verify the signature with the server's secret/key, check exp, then trust the claims — an unverified JWT is just a suggestion
JWTs can't carry roles — use a database lookup for every request
Accept any JWT with three dot-separated parts — structure implies validity
scenarios.hint: The payload is just base64 — anyone can mint one. What part proves the server issued it?
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability?
scenarios.situation: An API trusts the JWT role claim without verifying the signature.
scenarios.title: The self-issued admin token
scenarios.why: A JWT's payload is merely base64-encoded — anyone can craft {"role":"admin"}. Security comes entirely from verifying the signature (HMAC secret or public key) and checking exp/nbf/aud. Skipping verification turns the token into a client assertion. Rule: never trust claims from an unverified token; verify first, then read.

choices: A 30-day access token in localStorage — simple and long-lived
A short-lived access token (minutes) plus a rotating refresh token stored securely — compromise windows stay small
No tokens — HTTP Basic on every request
One permanent token per user, never expiring — rotation is complexity
evidence: # TODO: token lifetimes for the SPA
scenarios.hint: If an access token leaks, how long is it useful? What bounds that window — and how does the client get a new one silently?
scenarios.prompt: What is the sound token strategy?
scenarios.situation: A single-page app needs an auth token strategy.
scenarios.title: How long should a token live?
scenarios.why: Short-lived access tokens (5–15 min) bound the damage of a leak; rotating refresh tokens (single-use, replaced on each use, theft-detecting) let the client silently obtain new ones. Long-lived bearer tokens are bearer-everything — whoever holds them is the user for weeks. Rotation adds theft detection: reuse of a spent refresh token signals compromise and revokes the family.

choices: localStorage — JavaScript needs to read the token
A cookie with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax/Strict — HttpOnly keeps it out of JavaScript's reach (XSS can't steal what it can't read)
A cookie with no flags — flags are optional hardening
The token in the page's HTML — simplest
scenarios.hint: XSS runs JavaScript in your page. What storage keeps the token away from JavaScript entirely — and what new risk does cookie storage introduce?
scenarios.prompt: Where should the session token live?
scenarios.situation: The team debates localStorage vs cookies for the session token.
scenarios.title: Where does the token live?
scenarios.why: HttpOnly cookies are invisible to JavaScript, so XSS can't exfiltrate the token — localStorage offers no such protection. The tradeoff: cookies are sent automatically, so CSRF protection (SameSite + anti-CSRF tokens for state-changing requests) becomes mandatory. There's no risk-free option — only a chosen tradeoff: HttpOnly cookie + CSRF defense is the standard for session auth.

choices: Collect and store user passwords — you need them to verify identity
Use OAuth2 authorization code flow (with PKCE for SPAs): redirect to the provider, get a code, exchange it server-side for tokens — your app never sees the password
Ask users for their Google password and validate it against Google
OAuth is only for social logins — enterprise SSO can't use it
evidence: # TODO: 'Sign in with Google' for the SaaS app
scenarios.hint: Who should ever see the user's Google password — Google, or your app too?
scenarios.prompt: How should third-party login be implemented?
scenarios.situation: A SaaS app needs 'Sign in with Google'.
scenarios.title: Signing in with Google
scenarios.why: The authorization code flow delegates credential handling to the provider: the user authenticates with Google, your app receives a one-time code, and your server exchanges it (with client secret, never exposed) for tokens. Your app never touches the password. PKCE secures the flow for public clients (SPAs) that can't keep a secret. Storing or proxying provider passwords defeats the entire purpose.

choices: Log the user out everywhere on password change and rotate session ids on privilege change — sessions must be revocable server-side
Sessions can't be revoked — that's why JWTs are better
Store the session in a JWT so logout is client-side
Session ids never need rotation — they're random enough
evidence:
// sessions stored server-side in Redis, id in HttpOnly cookie
// TODO: logout and password-change semantics
scenarios.hint: The session record lives in your Redis. What does deleting it accomplish — and when should the id itself change?
scenarios.prompt: How should logout and password change work?
scenarios.situation: Server-side sessions need logout and password-change semantics.
scenarios.title: Killing a session
scenarios.why: Server-side sessions' superpower is instant revocation: delete the Redis record and the session dies everywhere — logout, password change, and 'sign out all devices' all work. Rotate the session id on login and privilege escalation to prevent fixation. (This revocability is exactly what stateless JWTs lack — hence short lifetimes and denylists there.)

choices: Run tests manually before pushing — CI is overhead
A workflow triggered on push/PR that installs, lints, tests, and builds — every change gets the same checks automatically
CI should only run nightly — per-push runs waste minutes
Commit directly to main and test in production — fastest feedback

on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

scenarios.hint: What breaks when checks are manual — consistency, or speed? What does the pipeline guarantee about every PR?
scenarios.prompt: What does the pipeline buy the team?
scenarios.situation: A team debates adding CI; currently tests run manually 'when someone remembers'.
scenarios.title: The pipeline that remembers
scenarios.why: CI makes verification automatic and uniform: every push and PR gets the same install/lint/test/build sequence, so 'it passed on my machine' becomes 'it passed the pipeline'. Manual testing decays under deadline pressure; per-PR automation catches breakage at the smallest possible diff. The workflow file is versioned with the code — the checks evolve with the project.

choices: Commit the key to the repo — the repo is private
Store it in the CI secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, etc.) and reference via env — secrets never live in source
Paste it into the workflow logs for debugging — logs are internal
Email it to the team — everyone needs it
scenarios.hint: The workflow needs the key but the repo is cloned everywhere. Where can the runner read it without it living in git?
scenarios.prompt: How should the deploy key be provided?
scenarios.situation: A deploy workflow needs a production API key.
scenarios.title: The key in the pipeline
scenarios.why: CI secret stores inject secrets as environment variables at runtime — masked in logs, never in git history. Committed secrets leak to every clone, fork, and CI log forever (and key rotation becomes archaeology). The rule is absolute: secrets enter through the environment, never through source.

choices: One Dockerfile stage that installs everything — simplest to read
Multi-stage: a build stage (SDK, dev deps) compiles the app, then a slim runtime stage copies only the built output — small, fast, attack-surface-minimal images
Docker images should include the full OS toolchain for debugging
Skip Docker — deploy the raw binaries

FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
scenarios.hint: The final image only needs to RUN the app, not build it. What rides along if you ship the build stage — compilers, dev deps, source?
scenarios.prompt: Why the two stages?
scenarios.situation: A Dockerfile uses a build stage and a slim runtime stage.
scenarios.title: Two stages, one image
scenarios.why: Multi-stage builds separate concerns: the build stage has the SDK and dev dependencies to compile; the runtime stage copies only the built artifact plus production deps. Result: smaller images (faster pulls/deploys), fewer vulnerabilities (no compilers in prod), and no source leakage. Single-stage images ship the entire toolchain to production.

choices: TLS is optional for internal tools — skip it
Terminate TLS at the reverse proxy/load balancer with a managed certificate (Let's Encrypt) — plaintext HTTP only inside the private network
Each app server manages its own certificate manually — full control
TLS slows everything down — disable it for performance
evidence: # TODO: HTTPS for the public-facing app
scenarios.hint: Who should own the certificate lifecycle — every app instance, or one edge layer? And who renews it?
scenarios.prompt: Where should TLS live?
scenarios.situation: A public app currently serves plain HTTP.
scenarios.title: HTTPS at the edge
scenarios.why: TLS terminates at the edge (reverse proxy/load balancer) with automatically renewed certificates — one place to manage the lifecycle instead of N app servers. Internal traffic stays in the private network (mTLS for the paranoid). Manual per-server certs rot and expire; 'TLS is slow' died with hardware AES and session resumption. Unencrypted public HTTP leaks credentials and content to every network observer.

choices: The homepage returning 200 — if it loads, the app is fine
A dedicated /health endpoint checking dependencies (DB, cache) with 200/503 semantics — the load balancer's routing decision needs the real signal
No health checks — the process manager restarts crashed apps
Log scraping for 'started' — the deploy log proves health
evidence:
services:
  api:
    image: myapp:2.4
    # TODO: healthcheck for the orchestrator
scenarios.hint: The process is up but the database is down. Which check tells the orchestrator 'don't send traffic here'?
scenarios.prompt: What should the health check verify?
scenarios.situation: An orchestrator needs to know whether the API can serve traffic.
scenarios.title: Healthy process, sick app
scenarios.why: A useful health check verifies dependencies (DB connectivity, cache reachability), not just process liveness — returning 503 when a dependency is down so the orchestrator stops routing traffic and can restart or replace the instance. The homepage 200 lies when the DB is down; log scraping isn't a signal. Distinguish liveness (is it running) from readiness (can it serve).

choices: Build once, configure per environment via env vars — the same artifact runs everywhere
Build a separate image per environment — each env's config baked in
Configure via code branches per environment — #if PROD
Environments should share one database — config doesn't matter
evidence: # image myapp:2.4 deployed to dev, staging, prod
scenarios.hint: If the image differs per environment, what are you actually testing in staging — the prod artifact, or a sibling?
scenarios.prompt: How should environment differences be handled?
scenarios.situation: The same image version deploys to dev, staging, and prod.
scenarios.title: One artifact, three environments
scenarios.why: Build the image once; inject environment differences (URLs, credentials, feature flags) via environment variables or mounted config. Per-environment images mean staging never tests the prod artifact — the thing you validated isn't the thing you ship. This is twelve-factor config: code identical, config external. The image is the unit of deployment; env vars are its parameters.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Fullstack as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The HTTP & APIs Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that HTTP & APIs is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in HTTP & APIs?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — HTTP & APIs issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — HTTP & APIs is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is HTTP & APIs supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any HTTP & APIs failure in Fullstack.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to HTTP & APIs
evidence: All HTTP & APIs components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Trace a Request Through the Full Stack
scenarios.situation: Users report the checkout page is intermittently slow. The frontend team blames the API, the API team blames the database, and the database metrics look fine. You have distributed tracing, per-layer latency dashboards, and a staging environment.
scenarios.prompt: Where do you start the investigation to find the real bottleneck?
choices: Increase API server instance count to handle the load, since slowness under traffic means under-provisioning
Pull a trace of one slow checkout request and walk it layer by layer — edge, frontend, API, queue, database — measuring where the time actually goes before blaming any layer
Add database read replicas, since slow pages are usually a database problem and replicas are the standard fix
Rewrite the checkout frontend in a lighter framework to reduce client-side render time
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Intermittent slowness with finger-pointing between layers is exactly what distributed tracing exists to resolve: one slow request's trace shows the time spent at each hop, turning blame into measurement. The other options prescribe fixes (replicas, rewrites, scaling) before diagnosing — each is expensive and each targets a layer that may be innocent.
scenarios.hint: Which option replaces opinions with measurements of a single slow request?
objectives: Use per-layer latency to localize bottlenecks
evidence: Checkout p95 latency 4.2s, intermittent, all regions
Frontend -> API -> database finger-pointing; DB metrics nominal

scenarios.title: Failure Propagation: When One Service Fails
scenarios.situation: The recommendations service starts timing out. Within minutes, the product page — which calls recommendations — slows to a crawl, thread pools saturate, and the entire storefront goes down. The recommendations service itself recovers, but the storefront stays degraded for another 20 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: What architectural pattern would have contained this failure to the recommendations service?
choices: More aggressive retries with no backoff on the recommendations client, so transient failures get papered over quickly
A bigger thread pool on the product page service so it can wait longer for recommendations without saturating
Synchronous health checks from the product page to recommendations before every call, skipping the call when unhealthy
A circuit breaker on the recommendations call with a fallback: after N failures the breaker opens, calls fail fast to cached/default recommendations, and the product page keeps serving
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The circuit breaker stops the bleeding: once the downstream service is clearly failing, calls fail fast instead of holding threads hostage, and the fallback (cached or default recommendations) keeps the page functional. Retries without backoff amplify the failure, bigger pools just delay saturation, and per-call health checks add latency without solving the coupling.
scenarios.hint: Which option makes the failure fail fast instead of holding resources hostage?
objectives: Contain downstream failures with circuit breakers
Prevent thread-pool saturation from slow dependencies
evidence: Recommendations timeouts at 14:02; storefront fully down by 14:09
Recommendations healthy at 14:15; storefront degraded until 14:35

scenarios.title: Cascading Retries and Backpressure
scenarios.situation: During a traffic spike, the API slows down. Clients retry failed requests immediately, which doubles the load, which causes more failures, which triggers more retries. The database connection pool exhausts and the whole system tips over — a classic retry storm.
scenarios.prompt: What combination actually breaks the retry-storm cycle?
choices: Exponential backoff with jitter on the client, bounded retries, and server-side backpressure: the API sheds load with 429 + Retry-After instead of accepting work it cannot finish
Unlimited retries on the client so every request eventually succeeds, combined with a larger database connection pool
Disabling all timeouts so slow requests eventually complete instead of failing and triggering retries
Caching every response for 24 hours so the database is never hit during spikes
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Retry storms need both sides fixed: clients back off exponentially with jitter (so retries don't synchronize into thundering herds) and give up after a bounded number of attempts, while the server applies backpressure — refusing excess work fast with 429 instead of queueing it until everything collapses. Unlimited retries, no timeouts, and blanket caching each make the overload worse or break correctness.
scenarios.hint: Which option fixes both the client's retry behavior AND the server's overload response?
objectives: Break retry storms with backoff, jitter, and bounds
Distinguish fast failure from silent queueing
evidence: DB connections exhausted at 19:44; full outage 19:47

scenarios.title: Fix the Markup
scenarios.situation: A page built entirely of divs and spans. Screen reader users report it as 'one long unlabeled region.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the remediation?
choices: Semantic rewrite: header/nav/main/article/footer, real headings hierarchy, labeled form controls, button elements — meaning in markup restores navigation for assistive tech and SEO
Add ARIA labels to all the divs
Add a 'skip to content' link only
It's fine — visual users are happy
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. ARIA on div soup is lipstick on structure failure — native semantics (button, nav, main, headings) carry behavior and meaning that ARIA can only approximate. Rewrite with semantic elements; use ARIA only where HTML falls short.
scenarios.hint: What does the screen reader need that divs can't give?

scenarios.title: Choose the Tool
scenarios.situation: You need: a 12-card dashboard grid (rows AND columns) and a navbar with spaced items.
scenarios.prompt: Which CSS tools?
choices: Grid for the dashboard (2D: explicit rows/columns), flexbox for the navbar (1D: spaced row) — dimension dictates the tool; most pages combine both
Flexbox for everything
Grid for everything
Tables — reliable since 1999
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Grid handles two-dimensional layout (dashboard rows × columns); flexbox handles one-dimensional distribution (navbar items). The dimension rule is the whole decision — forcing one tool into both jobs produces fragile hacks.
scenarios.hint: How many dimensions does each layout need?

scenarios.title: Survive the Phone
scenarios.situation: Desktop-perfect site; on phones the layout overflows horizontally and buttons are 24px.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: Mobile-first rebuild: fluid grid (minmax/fr), base single-column with min-width queries, 44px touch targets, test at 320px — horizontal overflow and tiny targets are architecture failures, not tweaks
Add <meta viewport> and hope
Shrink the font on mobile
Build a separate mobile site
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Overflow and 24px targets signal fixed-width desktop architecture — viewport meta alone can't fix it. Mobile-first fluid layout with proper touch targets is the rebuild; separate mobile sites died a decade ago.
scenarios.hint: Is the layout fluid or fixed — and what proves it?

scenarios.title: Pass the Contrast
scenarios.situation: Brand gray text (#999) on white fails WCAG (2.8:1). Designers love the gray.
scenarios.prompt: How do you resolve it?
choices: Data over taste: 4.5:1 is the AA minimum for body text — darken the gray to a passing ratio, keep light gray for large/decorative text only; accessibility requirements aren't design suggestions
Keep it — designers know best
Add a high-contrast toggle and ship the failing default
It's fine, most users see okay
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Contrast ratios are measured requirements, not aesthetic opinions — 2.8:1 excludes real users. Darken to passing, reserve light gray for non-essential text. Toggles don't excuse failing defaults.
scenarios.hint: What ratio does the text actually need — and what is it?

scenarios.title: End the !important War
scenarios.situation: Stylesheet has 40 !importants. New styles only work with more !important.
scenarios.prompt: What is the architectural fix?
choices: Specificity reset: audit and remove !importants, adopt low-specificity convention (BEM), introduce design tokens for the magic values — the war ends by disarming, not by bigger weapons
Add !important to everything new
Inline styles — ultimate specificity
Rewrite in a CSS framework
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Specificity wars escalate monotonically — the only exit is systematic disarmament: remove the !importants, adopt BEM's flat specificity, tokenize the magic values. Frameworks don't fix architecture; conventions do.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the next developer who doesn't use !important?

scenarios.title: The Layout That Breaks on Mobile
scenarios.situation: A marketing page looks perfect on desktop but on phones the hero section overflows horizontally, forcing sideways scrolling. Inspection shows a fixed-width 1200px container, several px-based font sizes, and an image with a fixed 900px width.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most robust fix?
choices: Detect mobile user agents in JavaScript and redirect to a separate mobile page
Set the viewport meta tag to width=1200 so the phone scales the desktop layout down
Replace fixed widths with fluid constraints (max-width: 100%, container queries or a max-width wrapper), use relative units for type, and make images responsive — then verify at 360px
Add overflow-x: hidden on the body so the sideways scroll disappears
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Fluid constraints and relative units fix the actual cause — content wider than the viewport — at every screen size, not just today's phones. overflow-x: hidden hides the symptom while content stays clipped; UA sniffing forks the codebase; a fixed 1200px viewport makes everything unreadably tiny.

scenarios.title: Fix the Waterfall
scenarios.situation: Page loads 3 independent API calls with sequential awaits: 900ms total, each ~300ms.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Promise.all: the calls are independent — awaiting them in parallel cuts ~900ms to ~300ms; sequential await on independent operations is the classic async performance bug
It's fine — 900ms is fast enough
Cache the results
Make the APIs faster
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Independent awaits in sequence pay the sum; Promise.all pays the max. 900→300ms with one keyword change. Caching and faster APIs help too, but the waterfall is pure waste — fix the free win first.
scenarios.hint: Do these calls depend on each other — what proves it?
objectives: Pay the max not the sum

scenarios.title: Survive the Missing Data
scenarios.situation: Production crash: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'city') — an API returned a user without address.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: Null-safe access (?. and ??) at the boundary plus API response validation — optional chaining prevents the crash, validation catches the contract violation; the bug is assuming the shape, not the missing field
Add if (user.address) everywhere
Tell the API team to never omit fields
Wrap everything in try/catch
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Two layers: ?. / ?? for graceful degradation at read sites, and response validation at the boundary to catch contract violations loudly. If-checks everywhere is noise; try/catch hides the shape bug; API promises aren't enforcement.
scenarios.hint: Where should the shape be guaranteed — at every read or at the boundary?

scenarios.title: Scale the Listeners
scenarios.situation: A 1000-row table with per-row delete listeners: sluggish, and new rows lack handlers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Event delegation: one listener on the table, match e.target to the delete button — handles current and future rows, one listener instead of 1000; per-item listeners are the scaling bug
Add listeners to new rows too
Paginate to 50 rows
It's fine — hardware is fast
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Delegation solves both symptoms at once: one listener (performance) that automatically covers dynamically added rows (correctness). Patching per-item listeners onto new rows treats the symptom and keeps the 1000-listener cost.
scenarios.hint: What breaks when row 1001 is added — and why?

scenarios.title: Kill the Desync
scenarios.situation: firstName/lastName inputs plus a separately-stored fullName — they disagree after edits.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Derive, don't store: fullName = `${firstName} ${lastName}` computed at render — the desync is structural (two sources of truth); derived state can't disagree with its source
Add an onChange that updates fullName too
It's a minor display bug
Store only fullName and split it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Duplicated derived state is a synchronization bug by construction — every update path must remember both copies. Deriving at render eliminates the entire bug class: one source of truth, zero sync code.
scenarios.hint: How many sources of truth exist for the name — and how many should?

scenarios.title: Find the Mutation
scenarios.situation: UI doesn't update after items.push(newItem) — the framework's change detection missed it.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what's the fix?
choices: Mutation blindness: push mutates the same array reference — change detection compares references and sees 'no change'; fix with immutable update ([...items, newItem]) creating a new reference the detector recognizes
The framework is broken
Call render() manually
Use a bigger state library
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Reference-based change detection can't see in-place mutations — same reference means 'unchanged' to the diffing algorithm. Immutable updates (new array/object) are the contract modern frameworks assume; violating it produces exactly this silent staleness.
scenarios.hint: Did the reference change — and what does the detector compare?

scenarios.title: The Race Condition in the Search Box
scenarios.situation: A search-as-you-type box fires a fetch on every keystroke. Users on slow networks see results for an older query overwrite the results for their latest typing — the UI shows answers to a question they already changed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: Make the fetches synchronous so they complete in order
Cache the first response and keep showing it until the user clears the box
Disable the search box until each request finishes, re-enabling on response
Tag each request with a sequence number (or AbortController) and only render the response matching the latest query; optionally debounce input so fewer requests fire
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Out-of-order responses are inherent to concurrent async requests — the fix is to identify the latest request (sequence token or aborting stale ones with AbortController) and ignore or cancel the rest, plus debouncing to reduce request volume. Synchronous fetch blocks the UI thread; caching the first response shows stale data; disabling input punishes fast typists.
scenarios.hint: Responses can arrive out of order — how do you ensure only the latest query's results render?

scenarios.title: Fix the Infinite Loop
scenarios.situation: useEffect fetches and setUsers on every render — infinite request loop.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Dependency discipline: the effect runs because a dep changes every render (or no array at all) — supply the correct dep array, or better, move the fetch into an event handler/query hook; effects synchronize, and this one re-triggers itself
Add an empty array and hope
Throttle the requests
It's the API's fault — rate limit it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The loop is structural: effect → setState → render → effect. Correct deps (or relocating the fetch out of the effect into a query library/handler) breaks the cycle. Empty-array-and-hope masks it until the next requirement changes the deps.
scenarios.hint: What changes every render that re-triggers the effect?

scenarios.title: Fix the Reorder Bug
scenarios.situation: Todo list uses index keys; after reordering, checkboxes attach to wrong items.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Stable keys: key={todo.id} — keys are component identity; index keys tell React 'position 3 is the same component' across reorders, so state (checkbox) sticks to positions not items
Reset checkboxes on reorder
Disable reordering
Use random keys
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Keys declare identity to the reconciler: index keys assert identity-by-position, which lies during reorders — component state follows the lie. Stable IDs assert identity-by-entity, and state follows correctly. Random keys are worse (remount everything).
scenarios.hint: What does the key claim is the component's identity — position or entity?

scenarios.title: Design the States
scenarios.situation: User list shows blank during load and crashes on API error. 'It works on my machine.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the professional fix?
choices: Tri-state design: loading skeleton, error state with retry, empty state — plus a data-fetching library for retries/caching; 'works on my machine' ignores the network's reality
Make the API faster so loading is brief
Hide errors — users don't need to see them
It's an edge case — ship it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Every fetch has three states; designing only success is designing for the demo, not production. Skeleton (perceived performance), error+retry (resilience), empty (clarity) — the library adds caching and dedup for free.
scenarios.hint: What does the user see during the 2-second load on 3G?

scenarios.title: Stop the Drilling
scenarios.situation: user prop drilled through 6 components; middle 4 don't use it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the refactor?
choices: Composition or context: pass the consuming component as children, or provide user via context — drilling through 4 indifferent layers couples everything to a prop they don't need
It's fine — props are cheap
Use a global variable
Merge the 6 components into one
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Prop drilling through indifferent layers creates coupling without benefit — every middle component now 'knows' about user. Composition (children slots) or context (provided value) delivers the prop directly to its consumer. Merging creates the mega-component anti-pattern.
scenarios.hint: Which components actually consume the prop — and which merely forward it?

scenarios.title: Profile Before Memo
scenarios.situation: App feels slow. A teammate wrapped everything in memo/useMemo 'for performance.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct approach?
choices: Profile first: measure with React DevTools profiler to find the actual bottleneck (usually data fetching, images, or one heavy component) — blanket memoization adds complexity and can hurt; optimize the measured hot path
More memo — it can't hurt
Rewrite in a faster framework
Blame the user's device
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Performance work without measurement is superstition — memo has costs (comparison work, code complexity) and the real bottleneck is rarely 'everything renders.' Profile, find the hot path, fix that one thing with evidence.
scenarios.hint: What did the profiler say is slow — and what did the memo actually change?

scenarios.title: The Effect That Fetches Forever
scenarios.situation: A component fetches user data in useEffect and stores it in state. The effect lists the state variable in its dependency array, and also sets that same state when the fetch resolves. The component re-renders in an infinite loop, hammering the API.
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimal correct fix?
choices: Add an empty catch block so errors don't trigger re-renders
Remove the state variable from the dependency array (depend only on the user ID), and guard the fetch so it runs when the identity changes — not when the data it produces changes
Wrap the fetch in a setTimeout so the loop runs slower
Move the fetch into the render body so it runs once per render
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The loop exists because the effect depends on the very state it sets: fetch resolves -> setState -> re-render -> effect re-runs. Depending only on the user ID breaks the cycle — the effect re-runs when the identity changes, which is the actual semantic trigger. The other options slow, relocate, or mask the loop without breaking it.
scenarios.hint: The effect re-runs because it depends on state it itself sets — what should it actually depend on?
objectives: Model effect dependencies on true triggers
Fetch on identity change, not data change

domains.summary: Components, hooks, data fetching, performance — building UI that scales.

domains.name: Node.js APIs: Server-Side JavaScript

scenarios.title: Unblock the Loop
scenarios.situation: API latency spikes: a report endpoint runs heavy PDF generation synchronously per request.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Offload CPU work: move PDF generation to a worker thread or job queue — synchronous CPU work blocks the event loop, stalling ALL requests; the loop handles I/O concurrency, not computation
Add more servers
It's fine — reports are slow
Cache the PDFs forever
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The event loop is single-threaded: one request's synchronous CPU work starves every concurrent request. Workers/queues move computation off the loop. More servers multiply the blocked loops; caching helps only for repeats.
scenarios.hint: What happens to other requests while one PDF generates?

scenarios.title: Fix the Contract
scenarios.situation: Mobile app breaks: API returns 200 with { error: 'not found' } for missing users; the app can't distinguish.
scenarios.prompt: What is the API fix?
choices: Correct status codes: 404 for missing resources with a consistent error body — 200-means-error breaks every HTTP client's assumptions (caching, retries, interceptors); codes are the contract
Document the 200-error convention
Return 200 with error: false sometimes
It's the app's bug — parse the body
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Status codes are the shared contract of HTTP — 200 asserts success to every intermediary and client library. Error-in-200 forces every consumer to implement custom parsing and breaks standard tooling. 404 + structured error body is the fix.
scenarios.hint: What does a 200 tell every cache, retry, and interceptor in the chain?

scenarios.title: Close the Token Hole
scenarios.situation: JWTs never expire. A leaked token from 6 months ago still authenticates.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Short-lived access tokens (15 min) + rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection — stolen tokens die in minutes, refresh rotation detects theft; non-expiring JWTs are permanent credentials
Make tokens longer — fewer logins
It's fine — tokens are secret
Ban the user and move on
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. JWT expiry bounds the blast radius: 15-minute access tokens limit stolen-token utility, rotating refresh tokens (with reuse detection) provide both UX and theft signals. Non-expiring tokens convert every leak into permanent access.
scenarios.hint: How long does a stolen token work — and what bounds it?

scenarios.title: Guard the Boundary
scenarios.situation: A crafted request with { age: 'old' } crashes the user-creation handler (NaN propagates to the DB).
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: Boundary validation: schema-validate every input (type, range, format) returning 400 with details — the database is storage, not a validator; NaN-in-DB is a validation-absent bug
Fix the DB to reject NaN
Trust the frontend validation
Sanitize in the DB layer
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Validation belongs at the API boundary: schema (zod/Joi) checks types, ranges, and formats before business logic runs, with 400 + error details for the client. Frontend validation is UX, not security — attackers skip the frontend.
scenarios.hint: What validates the request an attacker crafts by hand?

scenarios.title: Survive the Deploy
scenarios.situation: Every deploy drops in-flight requests — users see errors during the 30-second rollout.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM stop accepting new connections, drain in-flight requests, then exit — plus readiness probes so the orchestrator routes away before terminating; deploys shouldn't be user-visible events
Deploy faster — smaller window
Deploy at 3 AM
Retry on the client
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Graceful shutdown is the contract with in-flight work: SIGTERM → drain → exit, coordinated with readiness probes so no new traffic arrives during drain. 3 AM deploys and client retries mask the defect; draining fixes it.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the request that's mid-processing when SIGTERM arrives?

domains.summary: Event loop, REST design, auth, production readiness.

domains.name: Testing: Confidence to Ship

scenarios.title: Fix the Suite
scenarios.situation: Suite: 500 E2E tests, 45-minute runs, 20% flaky. Developers skip them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the rebuild?
choices: Rebalance the pyramid: convert stable E2E to integration/unit where possible, keep E2E to ~10 critical journeys, fix or delete flakes (no quarantined flakes), parallelize — 45 flaky minutes get skipped; 10 reliable minutes get respected
Run them nightly instead
Hire QA to maintain them
Delete all tests — they slow us down
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The suite's shape is the disease: E2E-heavy means slow and flaky by construction. Push coverage down the pyramid (fast, deterministic), keep E2E minimal and critical, and treat flakes as bugs — skipped suites protect nothing.
scenarios.hint: Which of these 500 must run in a browser — and which merely do?

scenarios.title: Test the Contract
scenarios.situation: Tests assert internal function calls; a refactor breaks 80 tests with zero behavior change.
scenarios.prompt: What is the test-design fix?
choices: Test behavior: assert inputs→outputs and user-visible outcomes, not implementation calls — refactoring must be test-safe; tests that lock implementation prevent the improvements they're meant to enable
Don't refactor — tests pass now
Update the 80 tests per refactor
Mock less
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Tests should specify the contract (given X, expect Y), not the implementation (calls function Z twice). Implementation-coupled tests punish refactoring — the activity tests exist to enable. Rewrite to behavioral assertions.
scenarios.hint: What should still pass after a pure refactor — and what does that imply?

scenarios.title: Bisect the Bug
scenarios.situation: Intermittent failure in production. Logs show nothing. The team guesses for the third day.
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined approach?
choices: Debug protocol: build a minimal repro (even intermittent ones reproduce eventually), bisect the search space (code, data, timing halves), verify each assumption explicitly — guessing is not a method; the protocol converts mystery into process
Add more logging everywhere
Restart the servers regularly
Blame the cloud provider
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Intermittent bugs yield to method: repro (load/stress the suspect path), bisect (halve code/data/timing), verify assumptions (the bug is always in an unverified belief). Logging helps but guessing for three days is the process failure.
scenarios.hint: What do you believe about this bug — and which belief is unverified?

scenarios.title: Gate the Merge
scenarios.situation: 'Urgent' PRs skip CI regularly. Production incidents trace to skipped PRs monthly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Non-bypassable gates: CI must pass for merge, no exceptions — the incidents are the cost of the bypasses; make the pipeline fast enough (15 min) that skipping tempts no one, and treat gate-bypass as the incident it causes
Trust senior devs to skip safely
Faster incidents response instead
It's fine — urgency matters
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The data is unambiguous: skipped gates → monthly incidents. Gates must be mandatory and fast — speed removes the temptation, mandatoriness removes the incidents. 'Trusted skippers' is how the incidents keep arriving.
scenarios.hint: What do the incidents have in common — and what would have caught them?

scenarios.title: Cover the Edges
scenarios.situation: Checkout works for normal carts. Production bugs: empty cart checkout, 1000-item cart timeout, expired coupon crash.
scenarios.prompt: What was missing?
choices: Edge-case testing: empty, boundary, invalid, and error states as first-class test cases — the happy path is the demo; the edges are production; each bug maps to an untested edge
More QA testers
It's fine — edge cases are rare
Add try/catch everywhere
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Every production bug listed is a classic edge: empty input, scale boundary, expired state. Edge cases aren't rare — they're where users live. Systematic edge coverage (empty/null/boundary/error) per feature prevents the pattern.
scenarios.hint: What are the empty, boundary, and invalid versions of this feature?

domains.summary: Unit, integration, and E2E testing — the safety net that enables speed.

domains.name: Deployment and DevOps

scenarios.title: Ship Safely
scenarios.situation: New checkout flow. Fear of deploy-day breakage. 100k daily users.
scenarios.prompt: Which strategy and why?
choices: Canary: 5% → 25% → 100% with automated rollback on error-rate/latency SLOs — blast radius contained, real-user validation, instant retreat; big-bang deploys gamble with 100k users
Big bang at 3 AM — everyone's asleep
Feature flag off, deploy, flag on for all
Beta subdomain — separate product
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Canary bounds the blast radius while validating against real traffic — 5% pain beats 100% outage, and automated SLO rollback removes human hesitation. 3 AM big-bangs just schedule the outage politely.
scenarios.hint: If this breaks, how many users feel it — and how fast do you retreat?

scenarios.title: Automate the Ship
scenarios.situation: Deploys: manual checklist, 2 hours, fails every third time, only one person knows how.
scenarios.prompt: What is the transformation?
choices: Pipeline as code: build→test→scan→deploy automated, artifacts promoted across environments, rollback one command — the 2-hour tribal ritual becomes a 15-minute reliable pipeline; bus-factor-1 deploys are organizational risk
Document the checklist better
Train a backup person
Deploy less often
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Manual deploys are unrepeatable, unauditable, and person-dependent — automation converts the ritual into a reliable system. Better docs don't fix 2-hour fragility; backups don't fix the process; deploying less often just batches the risk.
scenarios.hint: What happens when the one person is on vacation — and what does each deploy cost?

scenarios.title: See the Outage
scenarios.situation: Users report the outage 20 minutes before any alert fires. Alerts watch CPU and disk.
scenarios.prompt: What is the observability fix?
choices: Symptom-based alerting: RED metrics (rate/errors/duration) per service with user-impact thresholds, request-ID-correlated logs, distributed tracing — CPU/disk are causes; users feel symptoms; alert on what users feel
More CPU alerts with lower thresholds
A status page updated manually
Ask users to report faster
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Cause-metrics (CPU/disk) don't map to user pain — services can be down at 20% CPU. RED metrics on the request path detect what users experience; correlation IDs and traces make the 20 minutes diagnosable instead of mysterious.
scenarios.hint: What metric would have fired when users first felt pain?

scenarios.title: Seal the Secrets
scenarios.situation: An AWS key was committed to the repo 6 months ago. It's in git history. The key is still active.
scenarios.prompt: What is the complete response?
choices: Rotate immediately, purge from history (BFG/filter-repo + force-push with team coordination), scan history for others, move to vault-injected secrets, add pre-commit secret scanning — the key is compromised until rotated; history is forever
Delete the file — it's gone from HEAD
It's been 6 months — probably fine
Deactivate and create the same key again
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Git history is forever — deleting from HEAD leaves 6 months of clones with the key. Rotate (the only true revocation), rewrite history, scan for siblings, vault the secrets, gate commits. 'Probably fine' is how breaches happen.
scenarios.hint: Who has cloned this repo in 6 months — and what did they get?

scenarios.title: Prove the Retreat
scenarios.situation: The deploy pipeline has no rollback. 'We forward-fix.' Last forward-fix took 4 hours of outage.
scenarios.prompt: What is the requirement?
choices: Tested one-command rollback: previous artifact retained, rollback procedure drilled, automated on SLO breach — forward-fix under outage pressure is gambling; the deploy isn't complete until retreat is proven
Forward-fix faster next time
More staging testing
It's fine — outages are rare
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Rollback is the deploy's safety system: retained artifacts, one command, drilled procedure, SLO-triggered automation. 4-hour forward-fixes are the cost of its absence. 'Rare' outages are still outages — and untested retreats fail when needed most.
scenarios.hint: How long is the outage while the forward-fix is figured out?

domains.summary: CI/CD, environments, observability — shipping to production like a professional.

domains.name: Web Application Security

scenarios.title: Kill the Injection
scenarios.situation: Code review finds: query = `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user = '${req.user}'`.
scenarios.prompt: What is the verdict and fix?
choices: Blocker: string-concatenated SQL is injection by construction — replace with parameterized queries ($1 placeholders), add SAST to CI to catch recurrence; this ships over no objection
It's fine — user comes from our frontend
Escape the quotes manually
Low priority — internal app
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Concatenated SQL is the textbook vulnerability — 'our frontend' doesn't constrain attackers who craft requests directly. Parameterization is the fix; SAST gating prevents recurrence. Internal apps hold the same data attackers want.
scenarios.hint: What request could an attacker send that the frontend never would?

scenarios.title: Stop the Script
scenarios.situation: Comment feature renders with innerHTML. A test comment executes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the complete fix?
choices: Encode by default: textContent for text insertion, context-aware encoding elsewhere, plus CSP header as defense-in-depth — the PoC proves arbitrary JS execution in every visitor's browser; this is a ship-blocker
Strip <script> tags — good enough
It's just an alert — low severity
Moderate comments manually
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. alert(1) is the stand-in for session theft and defacement — the vulnerability is arbitrary script execution, proven. textContent/encoding fixes the sink; CSP contains the class. Blacklist-stripping (<script> only) is bypassed in minutes.
scenarios.hint: What could that script do besides alert — whose session is at risk?

scenarios.title: Harden the Login
scenarios.situation: Login: no rate limit, MD5 passwords, session in localStorage, no MFA option.
scenarios.prompt: What is the remediation priority?
choices: Auth overhaul: argon2/bcrypt migration, rate-limited attempts, httpOnly+secure+sameSite session cookies, MFA (TOTP/WebAuthn) — auth is the highest-value target; each gap is independently critical
Add a CAPTCHA — good enough
It's fine — passwords are hashed (MD5)
MFA is annoying — skip it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Four independent criticals: MD5 (cracked in seconds), no rate limit (brute force welcome), localStorage sessions (XSS steals them), no MFA (single factor). CAPTCHA doesn't fix hashing; MD5 isn't hashing anymore; MFA friction beats account takeover.
scenarios.hint: How long does each of these protections survive contact with an attacker?

scenarios.title: Set the Headers
scenarios.situation: Prod serves without CSP, HSTS, or X-Frame-Options. 'The app works fine.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the case for adding them?
choices: Free protections: CSP contains XSS impact, HSTS enforces HTTPS, X-Frame-Options blocks clickjacking — three response headers, near-zero cost, meaningful attack-surface reduction; 'works fine' isn't the security bar
They might break something — skip
Only big companies need them
Add them someday
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Security headers are the highest-ROI controls in web security: declarative, cheap, and they blunt entire vulnerability classes. 'Might break something' is tested in staging; 'works fine' describes functionality, not security.
scenarios.hint: What attack does each header blunt — and what does it cost to set?

scenarios.title: Model the Threat
scenarios.situation: New file-upload feature. Team wants to 'just build it.'
scenarios.prompt: What happens first?
choices: 30-minute threat model: what file types, what parsers, where stored, who can access, what's the abuse (malware hosting, XSS via SVG, zip bombs, path traversal) — then mitigations (allowlist types, scan, sandbox storage, random names) before code
Build it, pentest later
Allow only images — safe enough
It's internal — low risk
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. File upload is a top-tier attack surface (malware, XSS, traversal, bombs) — threat modeling before code is cheapest. 'Images only' still allows polyglots and SVG scripts; pentest-later finds the flaws after they're architectural; internal attackers exist.
scenarios.hint: What will the first attacker upload — and where does it execute?
