lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here, then each domain in sequence, then the mock assessment. Skipping ahead breaks the scaffolding the later material assumes.
What 'terminal' means: a terminal (also called console or shell) is a text window where you type commands. Every lab in this course runs there — no GUI needed.
Scenarios are decision drills: read the situation, commit to an answer, then study the explanation. The explanation is the real lesson.
Your progress saves automatically. A domain unlocks fully when you engage with its lessons, scenarios, and labs — depth beats speed.

example.code:
LEARN → PRACTICE → PROVE
  1. Read the lesson (concepts + worked example)
  2. Run the terminal lab (hands-on reps)
  3. Answer the scenarios (decision drills)
  4. Finish with the mock assessment (timed, exam-style)
example.walkthrough: This bootcamp mirrors how professionals actually learn: concept first, then hands-on, then judgment under pressure. Trust the sequence.

pitfalls: Skipping lessons and jumping straight to scenarios — the scenarios assume the lesson vocabulary.
Treating the terminal labs as optional — muscle memory is what survives exam pressure.
Rushing. Spaced, deliberate reps beat one marathon session.
lessons.try_it: Open the terminal now and type: echo ready — confirm you see your text echoed back.

lessons.title: Study Strategy for Full-Stack Web Development
concepts: Time-box your sessions: 50 minutes of focused work, 10 minutes off. Three focused sessions beat one exhausted six-hour grind.
Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close it and explain the key idea out loud in your own words before moving on.
The full-stack web development rewards pattern recognition. Every scenario you answer builds a mental library of 'I've seen this shape before.'
Track your weak domains explicitly. Revisit them with the systems-anatomy lens: trace the full flow, find where your mental model breaks.

example.code:
WEEKLY RHYTHM (example)
  Mon/Wed/Fri: 2 new domains (lessons + labs)
  Tue/Thu: scenario drills on prior domains
  Sat: timed mock assessment
  Sun: review misses, rebuild weak areas
example.walkthrough: Elite performers don't study more hours — they study with tighter feedback loops. Every wrong answer is a precise map of what to fix next.

pitfalls: Passive highlighting and re-reading — feels productive, builds nothing.
Avoiding timed practice until 'ready' — the clock is a skill, train it early.
Studying only strengths — comfort is the enemy of growth.
lessons.try_it: Write down your three weakest areas right now. You will re-test them at the end of this bootcamp.

lessons.title: Full-Stack Web Development: Field Overview
concepts: The big picture first: Full-Stack Web Development sits at the intersection of theory you must know and judgment you must demonstrate.
Employers and examiners test the same thing: can you reason from first principles when the situation is novel, not just recite facts?
Every domain in this bootcamp maps to a real capability: something you will actually do, decide, or explain on the job.
The capstone at the end proves you can integrate everything — that is the artifact you show, not just talk about.

example.code:
MAP OF THE TERRITORY
  Foundations → Core systems → Applied judgment → Capstone proof
  Each layer assumes the last. There are no shortcuts, only compounding.
example.walkthrough: Keep this map in mind as you work through domains. When a lesson feels abstract, ask: 'what real decision does this prepare me for?'

pitfalls: Treating domains as isolated trivia — they connect. Always ask how this domain touches the others.
Ignoring the 'why' behind procedures — procedures change, principles don't.
Waiting until the end to attempt the capstone — start scoping it now.
lessons.try_it: Skim the domain list for this bootcamp. Write one sentence for each: what real-world capability does it build?

lessons.title: How Assessment Works Here
concepts: Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts as complete — you prove it, then it counts. No click-through completions.
Scenarios are scored on judgment: the right answer with the right reasoning. Read every 'why' explanation even when you answer correctly.
The mock assessment is timed and cumulative. It draws on all domains — treat it as the real exam rehearsal.
Labs verify hands-on skill in the terminal. If a check fails, the hint tells you exactly what to fix — iterate until green.

example.code:
SCORING MODEL
  Lessons: completion requires passing the knowledge check
  Scenarios: attempts tracked, streaks build mastery
  Labs: all checks must pass
  Mock: scored like the real thing — this is your readiness signal
example.walkthrough: The system is designed so that 'complete' means 'can actually do it.' Respect the bar and it will carry you through the real assessment.

pitfalls: Gaming the knowledge check by guessing — it exists to protect you from false confidence.
Skipping lab hints — they are targeted coaching, not cheating.
Taking the mock once — take it repeatedly until your score stabilizes above target.
lessons.try_it: Answer this lesson's knowledge check, then run one terminal lab to feel the verification loop.

lessons.title: Capstone: Production SaaS Application — Blueprint
concepts: Your capstone proves integrated capability: Design, build, and deploy a complete SaaS application: authenticated multi-user app with database, API, payments integration design, tests, CI/CD, and production deployment.
Scope it in milestones, not monoliths. Each milestone is independently demonstrable — if you run out of time, you still have working pieces.
Document as you build. The artifact plus the write-up is what you show; either alone is half the value.
Build in public where appropriate: version control, clear commits, a README that explains the why, not just the what.

example.code:
CAPSTONE MILESTONES
  1. Define the product: users, core flows, data model
  2. Build the API: auth, CRUD, validation, error handling
  3. Build the frontend: routing, state, forms, responsive UI
  4. Add tests: unit, integration, and one E2E happy path
  5. Deploy: CI/CD pipeline, environment config, monitoring
example.walkthrough: A capstone is graded on integration and judgment, not just completion. At each milestone ask: 'what decision did I make here, and why this way?'

pitfalls: Scope creep — freezing the milestone list on day one protects you.
Building without documenting — you will forget your own reasoning within days.
Perfectionism on milestone 1 — get all milestones to 'working' before polishing any to 'great.'
lessons.try_it: Write your milestone list now, with a definition of done for each.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build Log & Documentation
concepts: Keep a build log: date, what you attempted, what worked, what failed, what you learned. This becomes your documentation draft.
Your README needs five sections: what it is, why it matters, how to run it, architecture decisions, and what you'd do with more time.
Screenshots and terminal transcripts beat prose for proving hands-on work. Capture evidence as you go.
Anticipate the three hardest questions about your capstone and write the answers before anyone asks.

example.code:
README SKELETON
  # Title — one-line value proposition
  ## Why — the problem this solves
  ## Quickstart — commands to run it
  ## Architecture — decisions and trade-offs
  ## Next steps — honest limitations
example.walkthrough: Documentation written after the fact reads like fiction. The build log keeps it honest — and honesty about limitations reads as seniority.

pitfalls: README as an afterthought — start it on day one, even as stubs.
Hiding limitations — naming them with a plan reads as maturity.
No reproduction steps — if they can't run it, it doesn't exist.
lessons.try_it: Create your capstone repo/directory and write the README skeleton today.

lessons.title: Capstone: Demo & Defense
concepts: Prepare a 5-minute demo: the problem, your approach, the working result, one hard decision you made. Rehearse it out loud twice.
Defense prep: for every tool and choice in your capstone, be ready to answer 'why this instead of the alternative?'
Connect each capstone decision back to bootcamp domains — this shows integrated understanding, not isolated effort.
End your demo with honest next steps. 'Here's what I'd harden for production' is the strongest closing line.

example.code:
DEMO ARC (5 min)
  0:00 — The problem (30s)
  0:30 — Your approach (60s)
  1:30 — Live working demo (120s)
  3:30 — One hard decision + trade-off (45s)
  4:15 — Next steps for production (45s)
example.walkthrough: The demo is a performance. Rehearsal is what makes it look effortless — and effortlessness reads as mastery.

pitfalls: Demoing without a fallback — have screenshots/video if live fails.
Over-running time — a tight 5 minutes beats a rambling 15.
Memorizing a script — know the beats, speak naturally.
lessons.try_it: Do a timed 5-minute dry run of your demo this week, even if the build isn't finished.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML
concepts: Semantic elements (header, main, article, nav) describe meaning — screen readers and search engines depend on them.
Forms: labels bound to inputs, fieldset/legend grouping, required and type attributes — accessible forms are usable forms.
The document outline: one h1, logical heading hierarchy — structure is navigation for assistive tech.
Validation: the W3C validator catches nesting errors — invalid HTML renders unpredictably across browsers.

example.code:
Article title

Content…

Meaning in the markup; presentation in the CSS.
example.walkthrough: Divs for everything — div soup is inaccessible soup.

pitfalls: Missing label associations — placeholder is not a label.
Skipped heading levels — h1 to h4 confuses navigation.
Div buttons — use <button>; keyboard support is free.
lessons.try_it: Mark up a blog post semantically: article, headings, figure, time element.

lessons.title: CSS Layout: Flexbox and Grid
concepts: Flexbox: one-dimensional layout (rows or columns) — nav bars, card rows, centering — justify/align axes.
Grid: two-dimensional layout — page structure, galleries — explicit rows and columns with named areas.
Choose by dimension: 1D → flex, 2D → grid — most pages use both, grid for skeleton, flex for components.
Responsive: media queries + fluid units (fr, %, minmax) — design for the content's breakpoints, not devices.

example.walkthrough: Memorize every property — learn the 20% that solves 80%: display, gap, justify/align, fr units.

pitfalls: Fixed pixel widths everywhere — breaks on real screens.
Float-based layouts in 2026 — flex/grid replaced them.
Media queries per device — design to content breakpoints.
lessons.try_it: Build a responsive page skeleton: grid areas that collapse to one column on mobile.

lessons.title: Responsive and Accessible Design
concepts: Mobile-first CSS: base styles for small screens, min-width queries upward — simpler than desktop-down.
Touch targets: 44px minimum — thumbs are imprecise; small targets frustrate.
Color contrast: 4.5:1 for text (WCAG AA) — check with a contrast tool, not your eyes.
Reduced motion: respect prefers-reduced-motion — animations that can't be disabled exclude users.

example.walkthrough: Design mobile-first; test with keyboard only and a screen reader at least once.

pitfalls: Desktop-only testing — 60%+ traffic is mobile.
Contrast by eye — eyes adapt; ratios don't lie.
Autoplay motion — vestibular disorders are real.
lessons.try_it: Audit a page: contrast ratios, keyboard path, reduced-motion, 320px width.

lessons.title: CSS Architecture
concepts: BEM naming (block__element--modifier): predictable class names that scale across teams.
CSS custom properties: design tokens (colors, spacing) — change once, propagate everywhere.
Specificity discipline: low-specificity selectors, no !important wars — architecture prevents the cascade from cascading.
Utility vs component: utilities for speed, components for consistency — pick per project, stay consistent.

example.walkthrough: Set up tokens before writing components — retrofitting is painful.

pitfalls: !important escalation — specificity debt compounds.
Magic values scattered — #2563eb in 40 places.
No naming convention — .thing2, .thing2-final.
lessons.try_it: Convert a stylesheet to tokens + BEM. Count the deleted magic values.

lessons.title: Modern JavaScript Essentials
concepts: const/let, arrow functions, destructuring, spread — the modern dialect; var is legacy.
Array methods (map/filter/reduce): transform data declaratively — loops for side effects, methods for transformations.
Template literals and optional chaining (?.): safer string building and null-safe property access.
Modules (import/export): organize code by concern — the module boundary is the architecture.

example.walkthrough: Write modern JS from day one — translating from var-era tutorials wastes time.

pitfalls: var and function-scoped surprises — use const/let.
for loops for transforms — map/filter express intent.
a.b.c without guards — optional chaining exists.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a legacy snippet in modern JS: const, arrows, destructuring, methods.

lessons.title: Async JavaScript
concepts: Promises: the async value container — then/catch chains; async/await is syntax over promises.
async/await: write async code that reads linearly — await the promise, try/catch the errors.
Parallelism: Promise.all for independent operations — sequential awaits on independent calls waste time.
Error handling: unhandled rejections crash processes — every promise chain needs a catch.

example.walkthrough: Default to Promise.all for independent calls — sequential is the exception.

pitfalls: Callback hell — promises/await replaced it.
Sequential awaits on independent calls — 3× slower.
Floating promises — unhandled rejections.
lessons.try_it: Convert a callback-based function to async/await with Promise.all.

lessons.title: The DOM and Events
concepts: querySelector/event listeners: the DOM API core — select elements, react to events.
Event delegation: one listener on a parent handles dynamic children — essential for lists.
Prevent default vs stop propagation: control form submits and event bubbling deliberately.
Minimize direct DOM manipulation at scale — that's what frameworks abstract; know the foundation anyway.

example.walkthrough: Learn delegation early — it's the pattern behind every framework's event system.

pitfalls: Listener per item — delegation scales, per-item doesn't.
innerHTML with user data — XSS; use textContent.
Forgetting preventDefault — forms reload the page.
lessons.try_it: Build a dynamic list with delegation: add, delete, no per-item listeners.

lessons.title: State and Data Flow
concepts: State: the data your UI derives from — single source of truth per concern.
Unidirectional flow: state → render → events → state — predictable beats clever.
Derived state: compute from source state, don't duplicate — duplication desynchronizes.
Immutability: new objects, not mutations — enables change detection and time-travel debugging.

example.walkthrough: Draw the data flow before coding — state bugs are architecture bugs.

pitfalls: Duplicated derived state — the desync source.
Mutation — breaks change detection silently.
Global everything — scope state to its concern.
lessons.try_it: Refactor a component: eliminate one duplicated state and one mutation.

lessons.title: Components and Props
concepts: Components: functions of props → UI — the composable unit; small, focused, named well.
Props flow down: parent → child, one direction — data flows down, events flow up.
Composition over configuration: children and slots beat prop-sprawling mega-components.
Keys in lists: stable unique keys — index keys break on reorder; keys are identity.

example.walkthrough: Keep components small — if it needs a paragraph to explain, split it.

pitfalls: Mega-components — 500-line render functions.
Index as key — reorder bugs.
Props drilling through 6 layers — context or composition.
lessons.try_it: Split a large component into three focused ones with clean props.

lessons.title: Hooks: State and Effects
concepts: useState: component-local state — the 80% hook; keep state close to its use.
useEffect: synchronize with external systems (fetch, subscriptions) — not for deriving state.
Dependency arrays: exhaustive-deps is correct — missing deps cause stale closures; the linter is right.
Custom hooks: extract reusable stateful logic — the composition mechanism for behavior.

example.walkthrough: Effects synchronize with the outside world — everything else is derived during render.

pitfalls: Effects for derived state — derive during render instead.
Missing dep arrays — stale closures.
Copy-pasted stateful logic — extract a custom hook.
lessons.try_it: Extract a custom hook from duplicated fetch logic in two components.

lessons.title: Data Fetching Patterns
concepts: Loading/error/data tri-state: every fetch has three states — design all three, not just success.
Libraries (React Query/SWR): caching, retries, deduplication — don't hand-roll fetch infrastructure.
Mutations: optimistic updates with rollback — fast UI, correct recovery.
Server state vs client state: server state is a cache (the library owns it); client state is UI state.

example.walkthrough: Adopt a data-fetching library — hand-rolled useEffect fetching accrues edge cases.

pitfalls: Only the success state designed — loading/error are afterthoughts.
Fetching in every component — deduplicate via the library.
Server state in global stores — it's a cache, treat it so.
lessons.try_it: Convert a useEffect fetch to a query hook with loading/error states.

lessons.title: Performance and Architecture
concepts: Render cost: components re-render when state/props change — keep trees shallow and state local.
memo/useMemo/useCallback: escape hatches for measured problems — profile first, memoize second.
Code splitting: lazy routes and heavy components — ship less JavaScript initially.
Folder by feature: co-locate components, hooks, and styles per feature — architecture that scales with teams.

example.walkthrough: Measure before optimizing — React is fast; the bottleneck is usually data or images.

pitfalls: Premature memoization everywhere — complexity without measurement.
One giant bundle — split by route.
State at the root — re-renders the world per keystroke.
lessons.try_it: Profile a slow interaction; fix the actual bottleneck with evidence.

lessons.title: Node.js Fundamentals
concepts: Event loop: single-threaded, non-blocking I/O — Node's superpower is concurrency without threads.
Never block the loop: CPU-heavy work blocks everything — offload to workers or services.
Streams: process data in chunks — files and network payloads without memory explosions.
The module system: clear boundaries, explicit exports — architecture at the file level.

example.walkthrough: Internalize the loop model — every Node performance bug is a loop bug.

pitfalls: Sync crypto/hashing in handlers — blocks all requests.
Loading huge files into memory — stream them.
Uncaught exceptions — crash without handlers.
lessons.try_it: Identify three loop-blocking patterns in a sample server; rewrite them.

lessons.title: REST API Design
concepts: Resources and verbs: nouns in URLs, HTTP methods for actions — GET /users, POST /users, not /getUsers.
Status codes: 200/201/204 success, 400 validation, 401/403 auth, 404 missing, 500 server fault — codes are the contract.
Validation at the boundary: reject bad input with 400 + details — never trust the client.
Versioning: /v1/ prefix from day one — breaking changes need a path that doesn't break clients.

example.walkthrough: Design the API contract before coding — endpoints are promises to clients.

pitfalls: Verbs in URLs — /getUsers, /deleteUser/5.
200 for errors — codes carry meaning; use them.
No validation — the database is not a validator.
lessons.try_it: Design a REST contract for a resource: endpoints, codes, validation rules.

lessons.title: Authentication and Authorization
concepts: Authentication (who) vs authorization (can): verify identity, then check permission — two distinct steps.
JWT: stateless tokens with expiry + refresh rotation — validate signature, check expiry, never trust claims blindly.
Sessions vs tokens: sessions for server-rendered, tokens for APIs/mobile — match the mechanism to the client.
Hash passwords with bcrypt/argon2 — never store plaintext, never invent crypto.

example.walkthrough: Threat-model auth from day one — it's the highest-value target.

pitfalls: Plaintext passwords — inexcusable, always.
JWT without expiry — stolen tokens live forever.
Auth without authz — logged in ≠ allowed.
lessons.try_it: Implement register/login with hashing and JWT rotation on a practice API.

lessons.title: Production Node.js
concepts: Environment config: 12-factor — config in env vars, never in code; secrets in a manager.
Logging: structured JSON logs with request IDs — grep-able, correlatable, shippable.
Graceful shutdown: drain connections on SIGTERM — deploys shouldn't drop in-flight requests.
Health checks: /health (liveness) and /ready (readiness) — orchestrators depend on them.

example.walkthrough: Production readiness is a checklist — run it before the first deploy.

pitfalls: Secrets in code — leaked in the first repo push.
console.log debugging in prod — structured logs or blindness.
No health checks — orchestrators fly blind.
lessons.try_it: Add env config, structured logging, graceful shutdown, health checks to a practice API.

lessons.title: Testing Pyramid
concepts: Unit (many, fast): pure functions and components in isolation — the base.
Integration (some): API + DB, component + store — the seams where bugs live.
E2E (few, slow): critical user journeys in a real browser — the confidence cap.
The ratio: lots of unit, fewer integration, handful of E2E — inverted pyramids are slow and flaky.

example.code:
PYRAMID
    /\ E2E: login, checkout (5)
   /--\ Integration: API+DB (30)
  /----\ Unit: functions (300)
Fast base, confident cap.
example.walkthrough: Write the test with the feature — later means never.

pitfalls: E2E-only suites — slow, flaky, expensive.
No tests on critical paths — the risky parts untested.
Testing implementation details — brittle tests.
lessons.try_it: Map your app's critical paths to pyramid levels; write the missing unit tests.

lessons.title: Effective Test Design
concepts: Arrange-Act-Assert: structure every test — setup, action, verification.
Test behavior, not implementation: assert outcomes, not internal calls — refactoring shouldn't break tests.
Edge cases: empty, null, boundary, error — the cases users will find.
Deterministic: no real clocks, network, or randomness — flaky tests get ignored, then deleted.

example.walkthrough: A test that never fails is a test that never protects.

pitfalls: Testing mocks instead of behavior — tautologies.
Time-dependent tests — flaky by construction.
No edge cases — the happy path lies.
lessons.try_it: Write AAA tests for a function including 3 edge cases.

lessons.title: E2E and CI Integration
concepts: Critical journeys only: signup, purchase, core workflow — E2E the money paths.
CI gates: tests run on every PR, failures block merge — the quality contract.
Test data: seeded, isolated, reset per run — shared state makes flaky suites.
Keep E2E fast enough to run: parallelize, scope ruthlessly — slow gates get bypassed.

example.code:
CI PIPELINE
  PR → lint → unit (2 min) → integration (5 min)
    → E2E critical (8 min) → merge gate
  15 minutes to confidence.
example.walkthrough: Green CI is a team habit — red mains get fixed immediately.

pitfalls: E2E everything — 2-hour suites nobody runs.
Skipped CI on 'urgent' PRs — urgency creates the bugs.
Shared test DB — order-dependent flakes.
lessons.try_it: Define the E2E list for your app (max 10) and the CI gate order.

lessons.title: Debugging Systematically
concepts: Reproduce first: minimal repro before theorizing — no repro, no fix.
Bisect: binary search the cause — half the code, half the data, half the time.
Read the error: stack traces point at the truth — read them fully before Googling.
Rubber-duck the assumption: state what you believe, then verify each belief — bugs live in unverified beliefs.

example.code:
DEBUG PROTOCOL
  1. Reproduce (minimal)
  2. Read the full error
  3. Bisect (halve the search)
  4. Verify each assumption
  5. Fix + regression test
  Discipline beats brilliance.
example.walkthrough: The regression test is the fix's proof — no test, no confidence.

pitfalls: Theorizing without repro — guessing.
Fixing symptoms — the bug returns.
No regression test — fixed today, broken tomorrow.
lessons.try_it: Apply the protocol to a real bug; write the regression test.

lessons.title: CI/CD Pipelines
concepts: Pipeline stages: build → test → security scan → deploy — automated, every commit.
Environments: dev → staging → prod, promoted not rebuilt — the artifact that passed staging ships.
Deployment strategies: rolling, blue-green, canary — choose by blast-radius tolerance.
Rollback: one command, tested — the deploy isn't done until rollback is proven.

example.code:
PIPELINE
  commit → build → unit/integration → scan
    → staging (E2E) → canary 10% → 100%
  Rollback: previous artifact, one command.
  Ship small, ship often, roll back fast.
example.walkthrough: Automate the pipeline before the team grows — manual deploys don't scale.

pitfalls: FTP-to-prod deploys — unrepeatable, un-auditable.
Rebuilding per environment — untested artifacts ship.
No rollback plan — forward-fix under fire.
lessons.try_it: Design a pipeline for your app: stages, strategy, rollback procedure.

lessons.title: Containers and Orchestration
concepts: Docker: the app + its dependencies as one image — 'works on my machine' solved structurally.
Images: minimal base, multi-stage builds, no secrets in layers — small, secure, fast.
Orchestration basics: desired state, health checks, rolling updates — the platform maintains what you declare.
12-factor apps: stateless, config-in-env, logs-to-stdout — container-native design.

example.code:
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
# Multi-stage: build deps ≠ runtime image
Small images, no secrets, stateless.
example.walkthrough: Containerize early — the discipline pays from the first deploy.

pitfalls: Secrets in image layers — history never forgets.
Latest tags in prod — unrepeatable deploys.
Stateful containers — pets, not cattle.
lessons.try_it: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for your app; scan it for secrets.

lessons.title: Observability
concepts: Logs: structured, correlated by request ID — the narrative of what happened.
Metrics: RED (rate, errors, duration) per service — the vital signs.
Tracing: distributed traces across services — the request's journey.
Alerts: symptom-based, actionable, owned — pages that wake people must matter.

example.code:
ALERT RULES
  ✓ p99 latency > 2s for 5m (user pain)
  ✓ error rate > 1% for 5m (breakage)
  ✗ CPU > 80% (cause, not symptom)
  Alert on symptoms users feel.
example.walkthrough: Instrument before you need it — observability is built in calm, used in storms.

pitfalls: Alerting on causes not symptoms — noisy, un-actionable.
No request IDs — uncorrelated log soup.
Dashboards nobody watches — instrument for alerts first.
lessons.try_it: Define RED metrics + 3 symptom alerts for your app.

lessons.title: Security in the Pipeline
concepts: Dependency scanning: audit on every build — vulnerable libraries are the common entry.
Secrets management: vaults and injected env, never in code — the pipeline handles secrets, developers don't see them.
SAST/DAST basics: static analysis in CI, dynamic scans on staging — shift-left, verify-right.
Least privilege deploys: pipeline credentials scoped minimal — the deployer can't destroy what it can't reach.

example.code:
CI SECURITY GATES
  npm audit (block on critical)
  SAST scan (block on high)
  Secret scan (block on any)
  Image scan before push
  Gates, not guidelines.
example.walkthrough: Security gates must block — advisory scans get ignored.

pitfalls: Advisory-only scans — ignored within a month.
Pipeline with admin creds — the blast radius.
Secrets in CI logs — printed for the world.
lessons.try_it: Add 3 blocking security gates to your pipeline design.

lessons.title: OWASP Top 10 Essentials
concepts: Injection: parameterized queries, never string concatenation — the #1 classic, still #1 cause.
Broken auth: MFA, session hygiene, rate-limited login — identity is the target.
XSS: encode output, CSP headers, textContent over innerHTML — untrusted data is code until proven otherwise.
Security misconfiguration: hardened defaults, minimal exposure — checklists per environment.

example.walkthrough: Threat-model every feature: what can the attacker control here?

pitfalls: String-built SQL — injection by construction.
innerHTML with user data — XSS by construction.
Default creds/verbose errors — free recon.
lessons.try_it: Audit a practice app for the top 5 OWASP items; fix each.

lessons.title: Auth Done Right
concepts: Password storage: argon2/bcrypt, unique salts — the algorithm handles it; don't innovate.
MFA: TOTP or WebAuthn — SMS as fallback only; phishing-resistant where possible.
Session management: httpOnly + secure + sameSite cookies, server-side invalidation — the cookie flags matter.
Rate limiting: login attempts, password resets — brute force needs a speed limit.

example.walkthrough: Copy the OWASP auth cheatsheet — don't design auth from intuition.

pitfalls: MD5/SHA1 passwords — broken decades ago.
JWT in localStorage — XSS steals it; httpOnly cookies.
No rate limits — brute force welcome.
lessons.try_it: Harden a practice login: hashing, MFA, cookie flags, rate limits.

lessons.title: Defense in Depth
concepts: Input validation: allowlist, at the boundary — reject what you don't expect.
Output encoding: context-aware (HTML, JS, URL, SQL) — each sink has its encoding.
Security headers: CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options — cheap, high-value, set them all.
Least privilege: DB users, API keys, file permissions — every component gets minimum access.

example.code:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000
X-Frame-Options: DENY
Three headers; meaningful protection.
example.walkthrough: Layer defenses — no single control survives contact with attackers.

pitfalls: Validation only client-side — attackers skip the client.
Missing security headers — free protections unused.
DB superuser for the app — one injection owns everything.
lessons.try_it: Apply headers + validation + least-privilege to a practice app.

lessons.title: Secure Development Lifecycle
concepts: Threat modeling: per feature, 30 minutes — what are we building, what can go wrong, what do we do about it.
Code review with security eyes: auth, input, crypto, sessions — the checklist for every PR touching them.
Dependency hygiene: audit, pin, update — the supply chain is the attack surface.
Incident-ready: logging for security events, runbooks — build the visibility before the incident.

example.code:
THREAT MODEL (30 min)
  1. What are we building? (data flow)
  2. What can go wrong? (STRIDE per flow)
  3. What do we do? (mitigations, owners)
  4. Did we do it? (verify)
  Lightweight, per feature.
example.walkthrough: Make threat modeling a habit, not an event.

pitfalls: No threat modeling — security by hope.
Security review only at launch — too late to be cheap.
Unaudited dependencies — the supply chain attacks.
lessons.try_it: Threat-model one feature end to end; file the mitigations.

lessons.title: HTTP Caching and Conditional Requests
concepts: Caching headers (Cache-Control, Expires, ETag, Last-Modified) let clients, CDNs, and proxies reuse responses instead of re-downloading them — cutting latency, bandwidth, and server load. Every cache decision is a trade-off between freshness and speed, and you must design that trade-off deliberately.

Conditional requests turn a full re-download into a cheap validation: the client sends If-None-Match (its ETag) or If-Modified-Since, and the server replies 304 Not Modified with an empty body when the cached copy is still valid.

Cache-Control directives encode different contracts: max-age sets a freshness lifetime, no-cache still stores but revalidates on every use, no-store forbids storing at all (use for sensitive responses), and must-revalidate blocks serving stale data after expiry.

ETags are opaque validators, usually content hashes. Strong ETags mean byte-identical content; weak ETags (W/ prefix) mean semantically equivalent. Never cache authenticated or personalized responses with public unless you can prove every variant is safe to share.

example.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
ETag: "5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592"

# Client revalidates before reuse:
GET /report HTTP/1.1
If-None-Match: "5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592"

# Server answers with no body:
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
example.walkthrough: The server tags the response with an ETag and a one-hour public freshness lifetime. On the next visit, the client sends the ETag back in If-None-Match. If the content is unchanged, the server returns 304 Not Modified — no body transferred — and the client reuses its cached copy, saving a full download.

pitfalls: Caching a response that contains user-specific data with public — one user's private data gets served to everyone. Personalized responses need private or no-store.
Using no-cache when you mean no-store — no-cache still stores the response and revalidates; sensitive data stays on disk. Know which contract you are signing.
Forgetting to version static assets — if you cache app.js for a year without a content hash in the filename, users run stale code after deploys.
lessons.try_it: Pick one GET endpoint you own. Decide its correct Cache-Control policy (public vs private, max-age, no-store) and justify it in two sentences, then add ETag generation to its handler.

lessons.title: Rate Limiting and API Throttling
concepts: Rate limiting protects your API from abuse, runaway clients, and cascading overload: it caps how many requests a caller can make in a window, returning 429 Too Many Requests when the cap is exceeded.

The three classic algorithms differ in burst handling: fixed window counts per interval but spikes at boundaries; sliding window smooths the boundary; token bucket and leaky bucket allow controlled bursts while enforcing a long-term average.

Always answer a rejected request with 429, a Retry-After header, and machine-readable limit headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset) so well-behaved clients can back off instead of hammering you.

Choose the limit key deliberately: per-API-key limits protect your quota, per-IP limits blunt distributed abuse, and per-endpoint limits shield expensive operations. Rate limits are a reliability feature, not just a security one.

example.walkthrough: This middleware caps each IP at 120 requests per minute on /api/. standardHeaders emits the RateLimit-* headers so clients can self-throttle. The custom handler returns 429 with a Retry-After hint and a structured JSON body, so both humans and SDKs understand they must wait 60 seconds.

pitfalls: Rate limiting only at the edge and nowhere in the service — a compromised internal client or a queue fan-out can still melt the database. Limit at the layer that owns the scarce resource.
Returning 429 without Retry-After — clients have no idea when to retry, so they retry immediately and make the storm worse.
A global limit keyed only on IP behind a shared NAT — an office of 200 people behind one egress IP eats one person's quota. Key expensive endpoints on API key instead.
lessons.try_it: Design a rate-limit policy for a public POST /signup endpoint: pick an algorithm, a window, a limit, and a key. Then write down how a legitimate user, a botnet, and your own mobile app each experience it.

lessons.title: State Hydration and Server Rendering Integration
concepts: Server-side rendering (SSR) ships HTML fast, then the client 'hydrates' it: React attaches event listeners and state to the existing markup. Hydration is where SSR apps most often break, because the client render must match the server render exactly.

Hydration mismatches come from non-deterministic rendering: Date.now(), Math.random(), locale-dependent formatting, or data that changed between the server render and the client render. Every one of these produces a different tree and a console warning — or a visible glitch.

Keep the serialized state contract explicit: the server embeds exactly the data the client needs (no functions, no class instances, no circular references), and the client validates it before trusting it. JSON with a schema check beats blind trust.
Suspense boundaries and streaming let you hydrate progressively: the shell renders first, slow sections stream in later. Design your page so the critical path never waits on the slowest data source.

example.walkthrough: The server serializes the page's initial state into a JSON script tag — plain data only. The client parses it once, runs it through a validation function (guarding against tampering or shape drift), and passes it into hydrateRoot so React attaches to the server-rendered markup instead of re-rendering from scratch.

pitfalls: Rendering timestamps or random values during SSR — server and client disagree, hydration mismatches, and users see flicker or broken interactivity. Render non-deterministic values only after mount.
Embedding secrets or full database rows in __STATE__ — that script tag is visible to anyone who views source. Serialize the minimum the page needs.
Hydrating the entire page as one unit — a slow widget blocks interactivity for everything. Split with Suspense so the shell is interactive while sections stream in.
lessons.try_it: Audit one SSR page you know: list every value rendered that could differ between server and client (dates, random ids, locale strings). For each, decide whether to make it deterministic, defer it to client-only rendering, or accept the mismatch — and say why.

lessons.title: Error Boundaries and Graceful Failure
concepts: In React, an uncaught render error unmounts the entire component tree — one bad widget can blank the whole page. Error boundaries are class components (or framework equivalents) that catch errors in their subtree and render a fallback instead.

Place boundaries at product seams, not just at the root: a crashing recommendations carousel should degrade to an empty slot while checkout keeps working. Boundary placement is an architecture decision about which failures are allowed to propagate.

A good fallback does three things: explains what happened in plain language, offers a recovery action (retry, go back, contact support), and preserves the user's context (form input, cart contents) wherever possible.
Errors caught by boundaries must be logged with context: component stack, route, user action, and the boundary that caught them. A silent fallback with no telemetry is a bug you will never find.

example.walkthrough: SectionBoundary wraps a risky subtree. getDerivedStateFromError flips the flag when a child throws, componentDidCatch sends the error plus component stack and route to telemetry, and the fallback ErrorCard offers a retry that resets the boundary — the rest of the page never unmounts.

pitfalls: One boundary at the app root — every error becomes a full-page crash screen. You have converted a localized failure into a total outage.
A fallback with no recovery path — 'Something went wrong' with no retry or navigation leaves the user stranded. Always offer a next action.
Swallowing errors without logging — the UI looks fine while data silently fails. Log every caught error with route and component context.
lessons.try_it: Map one real page into boundary zones: draw the component tree, circle each product seam, and decide the fallback + recovery action for each zone. Write the log payload you would emit per zone.

lessons.title: Client Data Fetching: Stale-While-Revalidate
concepts: Stale-while-revalidate (SWR) is the core pattern behind modern data hooks: show cached data instantly, re-fetch in the background, then update the UI when fresh data arrives. Users see content immediately and it quietly becomes current.

Cache keys are the contract: every distinct data view gets a stable, descriptive key (e.g. ['orders', userId, page]). Wrong keys mean wrong data shared across views; unstable keys mean the cache never hits.

Revalidation triggers — focus, interval, reconnect, mutation — keep data fresh without manual refetch calls. After a mutation, invalidate the affected keys so the UI converges instead of lying about state the server already changed.

Optimistic updates apply the mutation to the cache before the server responds, rolling back on failure. They make UIs feel instant, but you must handle the rollback path or users see phantom data that never existed.

example.walkthrough: The hook keys the order list on user and page so each view caches independently. revalidateOnFocus refreshes data when the user returns to the tab; dedupingInterval prevents duplicate in-flight requests. After creating an order, mutate invalidates the matching key, forcing a background refetch so the list shows the truth.

pitfalls: Fetching in useEffect with no cache key discipline — every mount refetches, race conditions multiply, and the UI flashes loading states the cache could have avoided.
Never invalidating after mutations — the user creates a record, the list still shows the old data, and they create it twice. Mutations must invalidate.
Optimistic updates without a rollback — the request fails, the UI still shows the phantom record, and support gets a ticket about data that 'disappeared.'
lessons.try_it: Take one list view in an app you know. Define its cache keys, its revalidation triggers, and exactly which mutations invalidate which keys. Then sketch the optimistic-update path and its rollback.

lessons.title: Background Jobs and Queue Workers
concepts: Background jobs move slow or unreliable work off the request path: email sending, report generation, image processing, webhooks. The request returns fast; the worker does the heavy lifting asynchronously.

A job queue gives you durability and retry semantics: jobs persist, workers pull them, failures requeue with backoff, and poison messages land in a dead-letter queue instead of looping forever. Without a queue, a deploy or crash loses in-flight work.

Idempotency is the non-negotiable property: a job may run twice (retries, duplicate delivery), so processing must be safe to repeat. Design job handlers as 'apply this effect once no matter how many times I run.'

Separate job types by priority and resource profile: a dedicated queue for latency-sensitive notifications and another for bulk batch work prevents a big export from starving password-reset emails. Monitor queue depth — it is your early warning for capacity problems.

example.walkthrough: The request handler enqueues a welcome-email job with five attempts and exponential backoff, using a deterministic jobId so duplicate enqueues collapse into one job. The worker checks a sent-flag before sending, making the handler idempotent — a retry after a crash never sends the email twice.

pitfalls: Doing slow work inline in the request handler — the user waits 8 seconds for an email send, connections pile up, and one slow dependency takes down the whole API.
Non-idempotent job handlers with retries enabled — every transient failure sends the email twice, charges the card twice, or creates the record twice. Retries demand idempotency.
One shared queue for everything — a bulk CSV import saturates workers and password resets time out. Isolate by priority and monitor depth per queue.
lessons.try_it: Pick three operations in a backend you know that currently run inline. For each: define the job payload, the idempotency mechanism, the retry policy, and which queue it belongs on. Identify the one that must stay synchronous and explain why.

lessons.title: WebSockets and Real-Time Channels
concepts: WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection to a persistent, bidirectional channel: the server can push updates the moment they happen instead of the client polling. Use them for live dashboards, chat, collaboration, and notifications — not for everything.

Connection lifecycle is the hard part: authenticate at handshake, heartbeat to detect dead peers, handle reconnects with backoff, and resume missed messages with sequence numbers or a catch-up query. Most WebSocket bugs are reconnect bugs.

Scale horizontally with a pub/sub backplane (Redis, NATS): any server instance publishes, the backplane fans out, and every instance pushes to its connected clients. Without shared state, a client connected to server A never hears about events on server B.
Backpressure protects you: if a client cannot keep up, queue with a cap and drop or disconnect the slow consumer rather than letting buffers grow unbounded and take down the process.

example.walkthrough: The handshake middleware rejects unauthenticated sockets before they join anything. Each socket joins a room scoped to its team, so broadcasts stay private. A shared pub/sub backplane lets any server instance publish an event that reaches clients connected to other instances; a sequence number lets reconnecting clients detect gaps.

pitfalls: No authentication on the WebSocket handshake — anyone can open a socket and listen on room names they guess. Authenticate before join, authorize every subscription.
No heartbeat or reconnect strategy — dead connections linger, presence shows users online who left hours ago, and mobile clients silently miss updates.
Broadcasting to all connected clients for targeted events — every client pays for every event and you leak data across tenants. Scope channels to the smallest audience that needs them.
lessons.try_it: Design the real-time layer for a team chat feature: handshake auth, channel scoping, the reconnect/catch-up protocol, and the backplane topology. List the three failure modes you consider most likely and how each is detected.

lessons.title: Service Boundaries and API Versioning
concepts: Service boundaries decide what can change independently: a boundary drawn around a real business capability (billing, identity, inventory) lets teams deploy and scale on their own cadence. Boundaries drawn around technical layers create distributed monoliths — all the pain of microservices with none of the independence.

Version your public API explicitly (URL path /v2/ or a version header) and never break existing clients without a deprecation window. Internal services can evolve faster, but anything a client or partner calls is a contract.

Deprecation is a process, not an event: announce with a sunset date, emit warnings in responses (Sunset header), track remaining callers, and only remove when usage is zero or the date arrives — whichever your policy states.

Backward-compatible change is a skill: add fields but never remove or repurpose them, keep enums open-ended, and treat every response shape as a promise. The cheapest versioning strategy is the one you never need because you never broke the contract.

example.code:
# v1 stays frozen; v2 adds without breaking v1
GET /v1/orders/42
{"id": 42, "total": 19.99}

GET /v2/orders/42
{"id": 42, "total": 19.99, "currency": "USD", "line_items": [...]}

# Deprecation signal on v1 responses
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Sat, 01 May 2027 00:00:00 GMT
Link: <https://docs.example.com/v2-migration>; rel="successor-version"
example.walkthrough: Version 1 keeps its exact shape forever — existing clients never break. Version 2 adds currency and line items alongside the old fields. v1 responses carry Deprecation and Sunset headers plus a Link to the migration guide, so remaining callers discover the deadline programmatically instead of by surprise.

pitfalls: Removing or renaming a field in place — every client parsing that field breaks at once. Additive changes only; removal goes through deprecation.
Versioning every tiny change — version sprawl is its own maintenance nightmare. Reserve new versions for breaking changes; evolve compatibly otherwise.
Announcing deprecation with no sunset date and no caller tracking — the old version lives forever because nobody knows who still uses it or when it may die.
lessons.try_it: Audit one API you know: list its last five changes and classify each as breaking, additive, or internal. For any breaking ones, write the deprecation plan you would have used: sunset date, signals, and caller-tracking approach.

lessons.title: Transactions and Concurrency Control
concepts: A transaction bundles multiple operations into one atomic unit: either all commit or all roll back. Without transactions, a crash between 'debit account A' and 'credit account B' leaves money created or destroyed.

ACID is the contract: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (invariants hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work), Durability (committed means survived a crash). Know which level your database actually guarantees.

Isolation levels trade correctness for throughput: read committed is the common default, repeatable read and serializable buy stronger guarantees at the cost of more locking and retries. Lost updates and phantom reads are the classic anomalies weaker levels allow.

Optimistic concurrency (version columns, compare-and-swap) scales better under low contention than pessimistic locking: read, compute, write only if the version is unchanged, retry on conflict. For hot rows, consider queueing or partitioning instead of fighting over one lock.

example.walkthrough: Both account rows are locked with FOR UPDATE inside the transaction, so no concurrent transfer can interleave and corrupt the balances. The debit, credit, and ledger entry commit atomically — a crash at any point rolls everything back, never leaving a half-moved $100.

pitfalls: No transaction around multi-step writes — partial failures leave the database in states your code assumed were impossible. If two writes must agree, they belong in one transaction.
Holding transactions open across network calls — locks pile up, throughput collapses, and deadlocks spike. Do I/O before BEGIN, keep transactions short.
Assuming the default isolation level is safe for everything — read committed still allows lost updates on read-modify-write cycles. Use optimistic locking or SELECT FOR UPDATE where it matters.
lessons.try_it: Find a multi-step write path in a system you know (order placement, user signup, funds transfer). Draw the interleaving that breaks it without a transaction, then write the corrected transaction with the minimal lock scope.

lessons.title: Migrations and Schema Evolution
concepts: Migrations are versioned, reviewable, reversible changes to the schema: each one moves the database from one known state to the next. They are code — reviewed, tested, and deployed like code.
Every migration needs a down path or a documented reason it is irreversible. The deploy that needs a rollback at 2 AM is exactly when you discover the down migration was never written.

Zero-downtime migrations follow expand-then-contract: add the new column (nullable), dual-write, backfill, switch readers, then drop the old column. Each step is independently deployable; the application tolerates both schemas during the transition.

Never let application code and migrations drift: the migration history is the single source of truth for schema shape. Test migrations against a production-like dataset — a backfill that takes 40 minutes on 10 million rows is a deployment plan, not a surprise.

example.walkthrough: The expand step adds a nullable column — old code keeps working. Backfill runs in batches to avoid long locks on a big table. Only in a later deploy, after all readers use display_name, do you add the NOT NULL constraint and drop the old column. At no point is the app incompatible with the schema.

pitfalls: Renaming a column in one deploy — old code writes to the old name, new code reads the new name, and the deploy window corrupts data. Expand-then-contract instead.
Migrations with no down path and no reversibility note — the rollback plan is 'hope we never need it,' which is not a plan.
Running an untested backfill on the production table — a full-table UPDATE locks for minutes, blocks writes, and pages everyone. Batch it, test it on a copy, measure first.
lessons.try_it: Plan a zero-downtime rename of a column on a table with 50M rows and constant writes. Write the ordered migration steps, the application deploy sequence between them, and the rollback story for each step.

lessons.title: Indexing and Query Performance
concepts: Indexes trade write cost and storage for read speed: a B-tree index turns a full table scan into a logarithmic lookup. The right index makes a query 1000x faster; the wrong (or missing) one makes the same query time out.
Read the query plan (EXPLAIN) before guessing: it shows whether the planner uses your index, how many rows it estimates, and where the cost concentrates. Optimizing without EXPLAIN is superstition.

Composite indexes follow the query's shape: equality columns first, then range columns, and keep the order matching the WHERE clause and sort. A composite index on (status, created_at) serves 'status = X ORDER BY created_at' but not 'created_at > Y' alone.
Every index slows writes and costs space — index the queries you actually run, verified by slow-query logs, not the queries you imagine. Drop indexes that no live query uses; they are pure tax.

example.code:
-- Before: full scan on 10M rows (EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- After: composite index matches equality + sort
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status_created
  ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at DESC);
-- EXPLAIN now shows Index Scan, 20 rows touched instead of 10M
example.walkthrough: The original query forced a sequential scan of 10 million rows to find 20. The composite index leads with the two equality columns (customer_id, status) and carries created_at in sort order, so the planner does an index scan touching only the 20 matching rows — the classic fix for 'slow list page.'

pitfalls: Adding single-column indexes for every column — the planner can only use one efficiently per query shape, and each index taxes every write. Design composites from real query patterns.
Indexing without checking EXPLAIN — the index exists but the planner ignores it (wrong column order, type mismatch, or low selectivity), and the query stays slow.
SELECT * with a perfect index — the index finds rows fast, then the heap fetch for all columns dominates. Covering indexes or selecting only needed columns finish the job.
lessons.try_it: Take the slowest query you know. Run EXPLAIN, identify the access path, and propose the minimal index change. Predict the new plan before applying it, then verify.

lessons.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Flows
concepts: OAuth 2.0 is authorization delegation: a user grants your app scoped access to their resources at another provider without sharing their password. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an identity layer on top — the ID token that tells you who the user is.

The Authorization Code flow with PKCE is the standard for modern apps: the client generates a code verifier, the user authenticates at the provider, and the client exchanges the code plus verifier for tokens. PKCE closes the code-interception hole that the plain code flow had on public clients.

Tokens have distinct jobs: the access token authorizes API calls (short-lived, least privilege), the refresh token mints new access tokens (long-lived, stored securely), and the OIDC ID token carries identity claims (never use it as an API credential).

Validate everything on your backend: verify the ID token signature against the provider's JWKS, check issuer, audience, expiry, and nonce. A token your server never validates is a string anyone could have typed.

example.code:
# Authorization Code + PKCE (public client)
# 1. Client creates verifier + challenge
verifier  = random_urlsafe(64)
challenge = base64url(sha256(verifier))  # S256

# 2. Redirect user to provider with challenge
GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=APP
    &redirect_uri=...&code_challenge=<challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256

# 3. Exchange code + verifier for tokens (server side)
POST /token { code, verifier, client_id } ->
  { access_token, refresh_token, id_token }
example.walkthrough: The client proves it is the same party that started the flow: only the holder of the original verifier can exchange the authorization code, because the provider recomputes the challenge from the verifier. An attacker who intercepts the code at the redirect cannot redeem it without the verifier, which never left the client.

pitfalls: Using the implicit flow in new apps — tokens in the URL fragment leak through history, logs, and referrers. Authorization Code + PKCE replaced it for a reason.
Accepting ID tokens client-side without server verification — signature, issuer, audience, and expiry must be checked by your backend against the provider's keys.
Requesting broad scopes 'just in case' — over-scoped tokens turn every token leak into a full account compromise. Request the minimum scope and escalate only when needed.
lessons.try_it: Map the login flow of an app you use: identify the flow type, where PKCE (or its absence) matters, which token goes where, and what your backend validates. Write the validation checklist your token endpoint would enforce.

lessons.title: Session Fixation and Hijacking Defenses
concepts: Session fixation is the attack where the adversary sets the victim's session ID before login (a link with ?sessionid=abc), then uses that same ID after the victim authenticates. The defense is simple and absolute: regenerate the session ID at every privilege change, especially login.

Session hijacking steals an active session ID — via XSS, network sniffing, or malware — and rides the victim's authenticated session. The layered defense is: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies, TLS everywhere, and binding sessions to reasonable signals.

SameSite=Lax or Strict on session cookies blocks cross-site request forgery from carrying the cookie; HttpOnly keeps JavaScript (and injected XSS payloads) from reading it; Secure ensures it never travels over plaintext. All three, always, on session cookies.

Detect hijack attempts with anomaly signals: impossible-travel logins, sudden IP/ASN or user-agent changes, and concurrent sessions from distant locations. Step up to re-authentication on sensitive actions rather than trusting the session blindly.

example.walkthrough: After successful authentication, regenerate() issues a brand-new session ID and destroys the old one — any session ID the attacker planted pre-login is now worthless. The session cookie carries all three protective flags so it cannot be read by script, sent over HTTP, or attached to cross-site requests.

pitfalls: Keeping the pre-login session ID after authentication — the entire fixation defense is this one regenerate call. Miss it and the attack works.
Session cookies without HttpOnly — one stored XSS anywhere on the domain hands every active session to the attacker. HttpOnly is non-negotiable.
Trusting the session for sensitive actions without step-up — changing email, password, or payout details on a possibly-hijacked session needs fresh authentication.
lessons.try_it: Audit a login flow you know: does it regenerate the session ID at login? List the cookie flags on the session cookie and the anomaly signals (if any) that would catch a hijack. Write the three fixes you would ship first.

lessons.title: Tokens vs Cookies: Choosing Session Storage
concepts: Cookies and tokens solve the same problem — 'who is this request from?' — with opposite trade-offs. Cookies give you browser-managed security semantics (HttpOnly, SameSite, Secure); tokens give you portability across clients (mobile apps, SPAs calling multiple APIs, service-to-service).

The classic secure web pattern is the HttpOnly cookie holding either a session ID (server-side session store) or a signed JWT (stateless). The browser attaches it automatically, XSS cannot read it, and CSRF is handled with SameSite plus anti-CSRF tokens for state-changing requests.

Storing access tokens in localStorage is the common SPA anti-pattern: any XSS on the page reads every token. If you must use tokens in the browser, prefer short-lived access tokens in memory plus rotating refresh tokens in HttpOnly cookies (the BFF pattern).

JWTs are not sessions: they cannot be revoked without a denylist, they grow with every claim you stuff in them, and 'stateless' just means you moved the state problem to key rotation and revocation. Use server-side sessions when you need instant revocation (logout everywhere, ban, role change).

example.walkthrough: The Backend-for-Frontend holds the real OAuth tokens server-side, keyed by the user's session. The browser only ever sees its HttpOnly session cookie — no token in JavaScript, nothing for XSS to steal. The BFF attaches the access token to downstream calls, and refresh happens server-side where the refresh token never reaches the browser.

pitfalls: JWT in localStorage 'because the tutorial did it' — one XSS vulnerability becomes a full credential theft with no revocation. Tokens belong out of script reach.
Stateless JWT sessions with no revocation story — 'logout' only deletes the client copy; the token stays valid until expiry. Banned users stay logged in.
Cookies for a native mobile app's API — no cookie jar semantics, manual header management, and CSRF protections that don't apply. Match the mechanism to the client.
lessons.try_it: For an app with a web SPA, an iOS app, and a partner API: choose the session mechanism for each client, justify it in one paragraph per client, and describe the logout-everywhere story for each.

lessons.title: Preview Environments and Ephemeral Deploys
concepts: Preview environments spin up a complete, disposable copy of your app for every pull request: reviewers click a URL and test the actual change instead of reading a diff. They turn code review from imagination into experience.

Ephemeral means lifecycle-managed: created on PR open, updated on every push, destroyed on merge or close. Without automated teardown, preview environments accumulate into a costly graveyard of stale infrastructure.

Data strategy makes or breaks previews: seeded fixtures give deterministic demos, anonymized production snapshots give realism, and each preview needs isolated data so reviewers cannot corrupt each other's state or leak real user data.

Guard the cost and the surface: cap concurrent previews, auto-sleep idle ones, put them behind authentication (they often contain unreleased features and real-ish data), and never let a preview URL reach production DNS or search indexes.

example.code:
# CI: build + deploy preview per PR, tear down on close
on:
  pull_request: { types: [opened, synchronize, closed] }
jobs:
  preview:
    if: github.event.action != 'closed'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: deploy --env pr-${{ github.event.number }}
              --url https://pr-${{ github.event.number }}.preview.example.com
      - run: seed --env pr-${{ github.event.number }} --dataset demo-fixtures
  teardown:
    if: github.event.action == 'closed'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: destroy --env pr-${{ github.event.number }}
example.walkthrough: Every PR gets its own namespaced environment with a predictable URL, seeded with demo fixtures for a deterministic review. Pushing to the PR redeploys automatically. Closing or merging the PR triggers the teardown job — the environment and its data are destroyed, so nothing lingers and nobody pays for it.

pitfalls: Preview environments with production data and no auth — an unreleased feature plus real user data on a guessable URL is a breach waiting for a crawler.
No automated teardown — six months later you are paying for 200 dead environments and nobody knows which are safe to delete.
Seeding previews with hand-built data per PR — reviewers test different things on different data and bugs slip through. Deterministic fixtures, seeded automatically.
lessons.try_it: Design the preview-environment policy for a team of 12: naming, data strategy, auth, idle-sleep timeout, max concurrent previews, and the teardown triggers. Estimate the monthly cost ceiling and the rule that enforces it.

lessons.title: Rollback Strategies and Safe Deploys
concepts: Every deploy is a bet; rollback is how you limit the loss. The strategy you choose — rolling, blue-green, or canary — decides how fast you can retreat and how many users feel the bad release.

Blue-green keeps two identical environments and flips traffic at once: rollback is a single switch back. Canary ramps traffic gradually (1%, 10%, 50%) with automated health gates — rollback is stopping the ramp. Rolling updates replace instances one batch at a time.

Database changes are the rollback killer: code rolls back in seconds, but a migrated schema does not un-migrate cleanly. Expand-then-contract migrations (additive first, removal later) keep every rollback path viable.

Automate the decision: define rollback triggers (error rate, latency p99, business metrics) before the deploy, not during the incident. A rollback runbook that requires three approvals at 3 AM is not a rollback strategy.

example.code:
# Canary with automated rollback gates
deploy:
  strategy: canary
  steps: [1%, 10%, 50%, 100%]
  gates:
    - metric: error_rate_5xx
      threshold: "> 1% for 5m"      # rollback trigger
    - metric: latency_p99
      threshold: "> 800ms for 5m"   # rollback trigger
    - metric: checkout_conversion
      threshold: "drop > 5% vs baseline"
  on_gate_breach: automatic_rollback  # no human approval needed
example.walkthrough: Traffic ramps in stages, and each stage must pass health gates before proceeding. If 5xx errors, p99 latency, or checkout conversion breach their thresholds for five minutes, the pipeline rolls back automatically — no 3 AM approval chain, no debate while users suffer.

pitfalls: Deploying schema-breaking migrations with the code — the rollback restores old code against a new schema and the app crashes harder than the bug you were fixing. Migrations stay expand-then-contract.
Canary without automated gates — the canary sits at 10% for hours while errors climb because nobody is watching the dashboard. Gates must act, not just alert.
Rollback tested never — the first time you run the rollback path is during a real incident, and it fails on a stale config. Rehearse rollbacks like fire drills.
lessons.try_it: Write the deploy-and-rollback plan for a risky release: strategy choice with justification, the gate metrics and thresholds, the database migration sequence, and the exact rollback command sequence. Then schedule the rehearsal.

lessons.title: Pipeline Security and Secrets Management
concepts: Your CI pipeline is production: it holds deploy credentials, signs artifacts, and can push to prod. A compromised pipeline is a compromised everything — treat its security with the same seriousness as the production environment.

Secrets never live in the repo: not in code, not in 'temporary' commits, not in build logs. Use the platform's secret store (or a vault) with least-privilege scoping — a frontend build job has no business holding the production database password.

OIDC federation beats long-lived credentials: the pipeline mints short-lived tokens to assume a cloud role per run instead of storing an access key that lives for years. No stored key means no key to leak.

Pin and verify everything the pipeline consumes: actions and dependencies by hash, base images by digest, and require signed commits on protected branches. A pipeline that builds whatever the internet serves today is a supply-chain incident waiting to happen.

example.code:
# OIDC: no stored cloud keys in CI
permissions:
  id-token: write   # mint OIDC token
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 # pinned by hash in real use
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-deployer
          aws-region: us-east-1
      # Short-lived credentials, scoped to the role, expire with the job.
example.walkthrough: The job requests an OIDC token from the CI platform and exchanges it for short-lived AWS credentials scoped to the ci-deployer role. There is no access key stored anywhere — nothing to rotate, nothing to leak in a log, and the credentials die when the job ends.

pitfalls: Long-lived deploy keys in CI secrets 'because it works' — they get copied, forgotten, and eventually leak. OIDC federation eliminates the stored credential entirely.
Secrets printed in build logs — a debug echo of an env var persists in log storage forever. Mask secrets and audit logs for accidental exposure.
Unpinned third-party actions (@v4 floating tags) — a compromised upstream release instantly becomes your compromise. Pin by commit hash and review updates like dependencies.
lessons.try_it: Audit one pipeline you know: list every secret it holds, who can read each, and which are long-lived credentials that OIDC could replace. Write the migration order, starting with the highest-blast-radius secret.

simulations.title: The CORS error
simulations.brief: The frontend at app.example.com calls api.example.com and the browser blocks every request: 'CORS policy: No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header'.

steps.symptom: Browser console shows CORS errors; the same API works fine from curl.
evidence: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy.
options: Recognize the split: curl has no origin policy, browsers enforce it — the API must send CORS headers for the frontend's origin
steps.explain: curl proves the API is healthy; the browser's same-origin policy is doing its job. The fix belongs on the server: declare which origins may call it.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: missing CORS headers on API responses.
evidence: app.use(cors());  // no options — reflects nothing specific
options: Configure CORS explicitly: allow https://app.example.com (and only it), with the methods and headers the app needs
Proxy everything through the frontend server
Tell users to install a CORS extension
steps.explain: Explicit allowlisting is the fix: the exact origin, the methods used, and credentials only if the app needs cookies. Wildcard-plus-credentials is forbidden by the spec.

steps.symptom: Fix applied. Verify from the browser's perspective.
options: Confirm the header is present on real responses and the frontend loads data without console errors
Confirm the header appears on 404s too
steps.explain: The header on a real response plus a clean console is the proof — curl can't verify CORS because curl never enforces it.

simulations.debrief: CORS errors are server-config issues wearing a browser's uniform. Allowlist the exact origin, never wildcard with credentials, and verify in the browser — not curl.

simulations.title: HTTP request lifecycle
simulations.brief: Restore the order of a full HTTP request lifecycle.

items: DNS resolves the hostname to an IP

simulations.title: Cookie or token?
simulations.brief: Choose the session mechanism for two clients of the same API.

steps.text: Client 1 is a server-rendered web app on the same domain. Mechanism?

choices.label: HttpOnly cookie session: automatic, CSRF-protected, revocable server-side
choices.feedback: Right: same-domain web apps are the home turf of cookie sessions.

choices.label: JWT in localStorage
choices.feedback: localStorage is XSS-readable; HttpOnly cookies are not.

choices.label: API key in the URL
choices.feedback: Keys in URLs leak into logs, history, and referers.

steps.text: Client 2 is a CLI tool scripting the API. Mechanism?

choices.label: Long-lived API token in the Authorization header, scoped and revocable
choices.feedback: Right: CLIs can't do cookie flows well — scoped tokens are the convention.

choices.label: The user's password on every call
choices.feedback: Passwords on every call maximize exposure and can't be scoped or revoked granularly.

choices.label: No auth — it's just a script
choices.feedback: Client type never determines auth need.

simulations.debrief: Same-domain web → cookie sessions; programmatic clients → scoped tokens. Match the mechanism to the client's constraints.

sections.heading: HTTP & APIs
items: Status codes are machine-readable contracts — clients, caches, and monitoring all branch on them. fetch resolves for any HTTP status — including 404 and 500 — and only rejects on network-level failures (DNS, refused connection).
REST — GET /users/7/orders with ?sort=-created_at&page=2&per_page=20 follows REST conventions: plural nouns, nesting for ownership, query params for filtering/sorting/pagination.

CORS is a browser-enforced policy — the browser blocks the frontend from reading a cross-origin response unless the server opts in via Access-Control-Allow-Origin (plus Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers on the OPTIONS preflight for non-simple requests).
REST design — consistent URL design is a usability feature of the API.
Resource modeling — 201 Created is the semantic status for successful resource creation, conventionally paired with a Location header pointing at the new resource.
Common trap — 200 is fine for creation; status codes don't matter to clients.
Common trap — the API's response lacks Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and the preflight needs the right Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers).
Common trap — CORS is fixed by adding mode: 'no-cors'.
Common trap — action verbs in the path are the REST convention.

items: Indexes — ('JOINs are slow' is a myth — missing indexes are slow; the join itself is the relational model's core operation.). Index-everything is wrong — indexes cost write performance and storage; the right index matches the query's access pattern.

JOINs — polyglot persistence matches stores to workloads: a document store fits the catalog's flexible, read-heavy shape; the relational database fits orders' transactional integrity (ACID, joins, constraints).
Aggregation — JOIN + GROUP BY with SUM is the database's home turf: one round-trip, set-based aggregation, the optimizer's choice of hash/sort strategies.
ACID — a single transaction makes the debit+credit atomic: either both commit or neither does (with rollback on failure) — the A in ACID.

sections.heading: Auth & Sessions
items: Password storage — server-side sessions' superpower is instant revocation: delete the Redis record and the session dies everywhere — logout, password change, and 'sign out all devices' all work.
JWT — a JWT's payload is merely base64-encoded — anyone can craft {"role":"admin"}. (This revocability is exactly what stateless JWTs lack — hence short lifetimes and denylists there.).
Signature verification — security comes entirely from verifying the signature (HMAC secret or public key) and checking exp/nbf/aud.
Token lifetimes — rotation adds theft detection: reuse of a spent refresh token signals compromise and revokes the family. Skipping verification turns the token into a client assertion.

Refresh rotation — short-lived access tokens (5–15 min) bound the damage of a leak; rotating refresh tokens (single-use, replaced on each use, theft-detecting) let the client silently obtain new ones.
Common trap — verify the signature with the server's secret/key, check exp, then trust the claims.
Common trap — ask users for their Google password and validate it against Google.
Common trap — accept any JWT with three dot-separated parts.
Common trap — one permanent token per user, never expiring.

Server-side sessions' superpower is instant revocation — delete the Redis record and the session dies everywhere — logout, password change, and 'sign out all devices' all work. Rotate the session id on login and privilege escalation to prevent fixation.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For HTTP & APIs: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Frontend Integration lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Backend Services terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
